lessons.title: Health and the doctor's office
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A1 you learned the body and how to say *Ich habe Kopfschmerzen*. This lesson takes you through a whole visit to the doctor: calling for an appointment, describing what's wrong and for how long, understanding the doctor's questions and instructions, and getting your medicine at the pharmacy. You'll also learn what to do in an emergency.

Three pieces of grammar make this possible:

- *seit* + dative for how long something has been going on: *Ich habe seit drei Tagen Fieber.*
- *sollte* and *müsste* for advice: *Sie sollten ein paar Tage im Bett bleiben.*
- the **[[imperative]]** in instructions: *Nehmen Sie die Tabletten dreimal täglich.*

## Illnesses and injuries

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *die Gesundheit* | health |
| *die Krankheit* | illness, disease |
| *die Erkältung* | cold |
| *der Husten* / *husten* | cough / to cough |
| *der Schnupfen* | runny nose, head cold |
| *die Grippe* | flu |
| *die Allergie* | allergy |
| *die Verletzung* / *verletzt* | injury / injured, hurt |
| *die Wunde* / *bluten* | wound / to bleed |
| *niesen* | to sneeze |
| *schwanger* | pregnant |

You *have* most illnesses, with or without an article: *Ich habe eine Erkältung. Ich habe Husten und Schnupfen. Sie hat Grippe.* An allergy is *gegen* something: *Ich habe eine Allergie gegen Nüsse.* — I'm allergic to nuts.

*verletzt* is an adjective: *Mein Knie ist verletzt.* — My knee is hurt. (In lesson 5 you learned the reflexive verb: *Ich habe mich verletzt.*)

When someone sneezes, Germans say *Gesundheit!* — literally "health!" — and the answer is *Danke!*

## At the doctor's

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *der Zahnarzt / die Zahnärztin* | dentist |
| *die Krankenkasse* | health insurance fund |
| *die Versichertenkarte* | health insurance card |
| *untersuchen / die Untersuchung* | to examine / examination |
| *das Pflaster* | plaster, Band-Aid |
| *der Verband* | bandage, dressing |
| *die Spritze* | injection, shot |
| *operieren / die Operation* | to operate / operation |
| *der Notfall* | emergency |
| *der Krankenwagen* | ambulance |

In Germany almost everyone belongs to a *Krankenkasse*. At the reception desk of a *Praxis* you're asked: *Haben Sie Ihre Versichertenkarte dabei?* — Do you have your insurance card with you? (Its official name is *elektronische Gesundheitskarte*, but *Versichertenkarte* and *Krankenkassenkarte* are what people say.)

The doctor gives you *ein Rezept*. You know this word from lesson 11 as a recipe; at the doctor's it means a prescription. You take it to the *Apotheke*. If you can't work, the doctor writes you off sick: *Der Arzt hat mich für drei Tage krankgeschrieben.* That connects to lesson 17: you *melden dich krank* with your boss, and the doctor's note confirms it.

### Emergencies

The emergency number in Germany and Austria and across the EU is *112* (*eins eins zwei*): *Rufen Sie einen Krankenwagen!* — Call an ambulance! When your practice is closed (at night, at the weekend) and it isn't life-threatening but can't wait, Germany has the medical on-call service, *116 117*, which answers around the clock. Hospitals have *die Notaufnahme*, the emergency department.

## seit: how long so far

To say how long something has been going on and still is, German uses *seit* + dative and the **[[present tense]]**:

- *Ich habe seit drei Tagen Husten.* — I've had a cough for three days.
- *Sie ist seit einer Woche krank.* — She's been ill for a week.
- *Wir warten seit einer Stunde.* — We've been waiting for an hour.
- *Er wohnt seit 2019 in Wien.* — He has lived in Vienna since 2019.

English uses "have had / have been … for / since"; German keeps the present tense, because the cough is still there. A memory hook: *seit* means it isn't over yet, so the verb stays in the present.

*seit* covers both "for" and "since": *seit drei Tagen* (for three days), *seit Montag, seit gestern, seit dem Unfall* (since Monday, since yesterday, since the accident). The noun after it is dative, so plural nouns add *-n*: *seit zwei Wochen, seit drei Monaten, seit vielen Jahren*.

The questions are *Seit wann …?* (since when) and *Wie lange schon …?* (how long already):

- *Seit wann haben Sie die Schmerzen?* — *Seit gestern Abend.*
- *Wie lange haben Sie schon Fieber?* — *Seit zwei Tagen.*

Compare *vor* (lesson 14), which points to a moment in the past: *Ich habe mich vor drei Tagen erkältet.* — I caught a cold three days ago.

## Advice: sollte and müsste

You met *sollte* in lesson 15. It's the standard way to give advice, from a friend or a doctor:

| | sollen → sollte | müssen → müsste |
|---|---|---|
| ich | sollte | müsste |
| du | solltest | müsstest |
| er / sie / es | sollte | müsste |
| wir | sollten | müssten |
| ihr | solltet | müsstet |
| sie / Sie | sollten | müssten |

- *Du solltest zum Arzt gehen.* — You should go to the doctor.
- *Sie sollten nicht so viel arbeiten.* — You shouldn't work so much.
- *Ihr solltet mehr Wasser trinken.* — You should all drink more water.

*müsste* is the **[[Konjunktiv II]]** of *müssen*. It is a little stronger than *sollte* ("really ought to") and often comes with *eigentlich* (actually, really): *Ich müsste eigentlich mehr Sport machen.* — I really ought to do more sport. People use it about themselves to admit something they don't do.

Notice the umlaut: *müsste* has one, *sollte* never does.

## Instructions: the imperative

Doctors, pharmacists and package inserts give instructions in the imperative, usually the *Sie* form with the verb first:

- *Machen Sie bitte den Oberkörper frei.* — Please take off your top. (*der Oberkörper* = upper body)
- *Atmen Sie tief ein. Und wieder aus.* — Breathe in deeply. And out again.
- *Legen Sie sich bitte hier hin.* — Please lie down here.
- *Nehmen Sie die Tabletten dreimal täglich nach dem Essen.* — Take the tablets three times a day after meals.
- *Kommen Sie in einer Woche wieder.* — Come back in a week.

Between friends and in the family, use the *du* form (no *-st*, no *du*): *Bleib im Bett! Trink viel Tee! Nimm eine Tablette! Iss etwas!* Remember the stem-changing verbs: *nehmen → nimm*, *essen → iss*.

## How often?

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *täglich* | daily |
| *wöchentlich* | weekly |
| *monatlich* | monthly |
| *einmal / zweimal / dreimal täglich* | once / twice / three times a day |
| *morgens, mittags, abends* | in the morning(s), at midday, in the evening(s) |
| *alle vier Stunden* | every four hours |
| *vor / nach dem Essen* | before / after meals |

*täglich* and *wöchentlich* are adjectives too: *eine tägliche Tablette*, *die wöchentliche Untersuchung*. *alle* + time + plural means "every": *alle zwei Tage*.

## Dialogue: at the doctor's

Tom has been feeling ill for a few days. He sees Dr. Lehmann.

> Dr. Lehmann: Guten Tag, Herr Fischer. Was fehlt Ihnen denn?
>
> Tom: Ich habe seit vier Tagen Husten und Schnupfen, und seit gestern habe ich auch Fieber. Ich bin total müde.
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Wie hoch ist das Fieber?
>
> Tom: Heute Morgen hatte ich 38,5.
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Hm. Machen Sie bitte den Oberkörper frei, ich möchte Sie untersuchen … Atmen Sie tief ein … und aus. Husten Sie bitte einmal.
>
> Tom: Ist es eine Grippe?
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Nein, zum Glück nicht. Es ist eine starke Erkältung. Haben Sie Allergien gegen Medikamente?
>
> Tom: Nein, ich habe keine Allergien.
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Gut. Ich gebe Ihnen ein Rezept für einen Hustensaft. Nehmen Sie ihn dreimal täglich nach dem Essen. Sie sollten viel trinken und ein paar Tage im Bett bleiben.
>
> Tom: Ich müsste eigentlich morgen arbeiten …
>
> Dr. Lehmann: Das geht nicht. Ich schreibe Sie bis Freitag krank. Wenn das Fieber nicht besser wird, kommen Sie bitte wieder.
>
> Tom: Vielen Dank, Frau Doktor.

In English:

> Dr Lehmann: Hello, Mr Fischer. So what's the matter?
>
> Tom: I've had a cough and a runny nose for four days, and since yesterday I've also had a temperature. I'm completely exhausted.
>
> Dr Lehmann: How high is the temperature?
>
> Tom: This morning it was 38.5.
>
> Dr Lehmann: Hm. Please take off your top, I'd like to examine you … Breathe in deeply … and out. Please cough once.
>
> Tom: Is it flu?
>
> Dr Lehmann: No, luckily not. It's a bad cold. Are you allergic to any medicines?
>
> Tom: No, I don't have any allergies.
>
> Dr Lehmann: Good. I'll give you a prescription for cough syrup. Take it three times a day after meals. You should drink a lot and stay in bed for a few days.
>
> Tom: I'm actually supposed to work tomorrow …
>
> Dr Lehmann: That's not possible. I'm signing you off sick until Friday. If the fever doesn't get better, please come back.
>
> Tom: Thank you very much, doctor.

*Was fehlt Ihnen?* (literally "What is missing to you?") is the classic doctor's question, with the dative verb *fehlen* from lesson 7. Germans give their temperature in degrees Celsius and say *achtunddreißig fünf*. A woman doctor is addressed as *Frau Doktor*, a man as *Herr Doktor*.

## A notice in the waiting room

> Liebe Patientinnen und Patienten, bitte bringen Sie zu jedem Termin Ihre Versichertenkarte mit. Wenn Sie Fieber oder starken Husten haben, melden Sie sich bitte vorher telefonisch an. Bei einem Notfall rufen Sie die 112. Die Praxis ist mittwochs nachmittags geschlossen.

Dear patients, please bring your insurance card to every appointment. If you have a temperature or a bad cough, please let us know by phone in advance. In an emergency, call 112. The practice is closed on Wednesday afternoons.

## Pronunciation

- *Husten*: long *u*, HUU-sten. *husten* (the verb) sounds the same.
- *Schnupfen*: the *pf* is one quick sound, lips closed, then *f*: SCHNUP-fen.
- *Allergie*: stress on the last syllable, al-ler-GIE. The *g* is hard, as in "go".
- *Operation*: o-pe-ra-TSION, the *-tion* is "tsion".
- *niesen*: long *ie*, and the *s* between vowels is voiced like English *z*: NEE-zen.
- *müsste*: short *ü*; don't confuse it with *musste* (had to, past).

## Common mistakes

- *Ich habe Husten seit drei Tagen gehabt.* — German uses the present with *seit*: *Ich habe seit drei Tagen Husten.*
- *seit drei Tage* — Dative plural adds *-n*: *seit drei Tagen*.
- *Ich bin krank für eine Woche* to mean "I've been ill for a week" — use *seit*: *Ich bin seit einer Woche krank.* (*für* is for a planned period: *Ich bin für eine Woche in Berlin.*)
- *Du sollst zum Arzt gehen* is an order someone gave ("you're supposed to"). Advice is *Du solltest zum Arzt gehen.*
- *Nimmst die Tablette!* — The *du* imperative drops *-st*: *Nimm die Tablette!*
- *Ich habe eine Allergie für Katzen.* — Use *gegen*: *eine Allergie gegen Katzen*.
- *Mein Arm ist verletzen.* — After *sein* use the adjective: *Mein Arm ist verletzt.*

## Key points

- *seit* + dative + present tense for something that started in the past and is still going on: *Ich habe seit drei Tagen Fieber.* Questions: *Seit wann …? Wie lange schon …?*
- Advice: *Du solltest / Sie sollten …*; stronger or self-critical: *Ich müsste eigentlich …*
- Instructions use the imperative: *Nehmen Sie …*, *Atmen Sie ein*; with friends *Bleib im Bett! Nimm …!*
- Frequency: *täglich, wöchentlich, dreimal täglich, alle vier Stunden*.
- *Was fehlt Ihnen? Ich habe eine Erkältung / Husten / Schnupfen / Grippe.* *Gesundheit!* after a sneeze.
- Bring the *Versichertenkarte*; the doctor writes *ein Rezept* and may sign you off sick. Emergency: *112*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Media, technology and relative clauses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can already say a lot about the things around you: *Ich habe ein neues Handy. Es ist sehr schnell.* But that takes two sentences, and real speech packs the description into one: "I have a new phone that is very fast." The word "that" (or "which", "who") starts a **[[relative clause]]**, a clause that describes a noun. Relative clauses let you describe people (*die Frau, die neben mir wohnt*), explain words you don't know and add details without starting a new sentence.

The good news: you already know the hard part. A relative clause is a **[[subordinate clause]]**, so the verb goes to the end, exactly as after *weil*, *dass* and *wenn* (lessons 3 and 4). And the words that start it look almost exactly like *der, die, das*.

The theme is media and technology: the internet, computers, television and the press, where people constantly explain which device, app or programme they mean.

## Words for screens and media

| German | English |
|---|---|
| das Internet, online | the internet, online |
| das Netz, das WLAN | the net / network, Wi-Fi |
| die Webseite | web page, website |
| die App, das Programm | app, (computer) program |
| der Laptop, der Bildschirm, die Tastatur | laptop, screen, keyboard |
| das Passwort, sich einloggen | password, to log in |
| herunterladen, hochladen | to download, to upload |
| speichern, löschen | to save, to delete |
| aufnehmen | to record |
| das Video, der Kommentar | video, comment |
| das Fernsehen, das Radio, die Sendung | television, radio, programme / broadcast |
| die Nachrichten | the news |
| die Zeitschrift, der Artikel, der Bericht | magazine, article, report |
| die Werbung | advertising, advert |

A few notes:

- *das Programm* is a computer program, but also a TV channel or a TV schedule: *Was kommt heute im Programm?* — What's on today? One show is *die Sendung*.
- *das Fernsehen* is television as a medium (*im Fernsehen* — on TV); the device is *der Fernseher*.
- *die Nachrichten* (plural) are the news: *Hast du die Nachrichten gehört?* In the singular, *die Nachricht* is a message, as in A1.
- *herunterladen* and *hochladen* are separable, and *laden* changes its vowel like *fahren*: *Ich lade die App herunter. Er lädt ein Video hoch.* Perfect: *hat heruntergeladen, hat hochgeladen*.
- *aufnehmen* is separable and works like *nehmen*: *Sie nimmt die Sendung auf* — she's recording the programme; *hat aufgenommen*.
- *sich einloggen* is reflexive (lesson 5): *Ich logge mich ein. Hast du dich schon eingeloggt?*

## What a relative clause does

Compare these two ways of saying the same thing:

- *Ich habe einen Laptop. Der Laptop ist sehr leicht.* — I have a laptop. The laptop is very light.
- *Ich habe einen Laptop, der sehr leicht ist.* — I have a laptop that is very light.

*Ich habe einen Laptop* is the **[[main clause]]**; it could stand alone. *der sehr leicht ist* is the relative clause; it only describes *Laptop*. The noun it describes is the **[[antecedent]]**, and the word that starts it, here *der*, is the **[[relative pronoun]]**, which stands for the antecedent inside the relative clause.

Three rules make a German relative clause:

1. The relative pronoun comes first in the relative clause.
2. The conjugated verb goes to the very end.
3. Commas separate the relative clause from the rest of the sentence, always.

English can sometimes drop "that" (*the film I saw*). German never drops the relative pronoun: *der Film, den ich gesehen habe*.

## The relative pronouns: nominative

The relative pronouns are the same as the definite article in the nominative and accusative. In the nominative you use them when the antecedent is the subject of the relative clause, the one doing the action.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | der | die | das | die |

- *Das ist der Kollege, der unsere Webseite macht.* — That's the colleague who does our website.
- *Ich lese eine Zeitschrift, die jeden Monat erscheint.* — I read a magazine that comes out every month. (*erscheinen* = to appear, to come out)
- *Wo ist das Kabel, das neben dem Bildschirm lag?* — Where's the cable that was lying next to the screen?
- *Ich mag Sendungen, die nicht so lang sind.* — I like programmes that aren't so long.

In each relative clause, ask: who or what does the action? *Der* (= the colleague) makes the website; *die* (= the magazine) comes out every month. So the relative pronoun is the subject, and the subject is nominative.

## The accusative

When the antecedent is the direct object inside the relative clause, the relative pronoun is accusative. As with the articles, only the masculine changes: *der* becomes *den*.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | der | die | das | die |
| accusative | den | die | das | die |

- *Der Laptop, den ich gekauft habe, war nicht teuer.* — The laptop I bought wasn't expensive.
- *Kennst du die App, die alle benutzen?* — Do you know the app everybody uses?
- *Das Video, das du hochgeladen hast, ist super.* — The video you uploaded is great.
- *Wo sind die Fotos, die wir im Urlaub gemacht haben?* — Where are the photos we took on holiday?

In *den ich gekauft habe*, the subject is *ich*; the laptop is the thing bought, the object. So: accusative, *den*.

### Choosing the right pronoun: two questions

This is the key idea of the whole lesson. You need two pieces of information, and they come from two different places:

1. Gender and number come from the antecedent, the noun before the comma. *der Bericht* → masculine. *die Nachrichten* → plural.
2. Case comes from the job the pronoun does inside its own clause, after the comma. Subject → nominative. Direct object → accusative.

Look at the same noun in two different jobs:

- *Das ist der Artikel, der gestern online war.* — That's the article that was online yesterday. (The article was online: subject → *der*.)
- *Das ist der Artikel, den ich dir geschickt habe.* — That's the article I sent you. (I sent it: object → *den*.)

A memory hook: gender looks back, case looks inside.

The case of the antecedent in the main clause doesn't matter: in *Ich habe einen Laptop, der sehr leicht ist*, the main clause has *einen*, but inside its own clause the laptop is the subject, so: *der*.

## Word order inside the relative clause

The verb goes to the end, as in every subordinate clause. That has the usual consequences:

- Perfect: the auxiliary comes last, after the participle: *die Mail, die ich gestern geschrieben habe*.
- Separable verbs join up again at the end: *das Programm, das ich gerade herunterlade*; *die Sendung, die um acht anfängt*.
- Modal verbs come last, after the infinitive: *ein Passwort, das man nicht vergessen kann*; *Dateien, die du löschen musst* (*die Datei* = file).
- Reflexive pronouns come early, right after the relative pronoun: *die Nachbarin, die sich nie einloggen kann* — the neighbour who can never log in.

### A relative clause in the middle

The relative clause comes straight after its antecedent. If the antecedent is at the start of the sentence, the relative clause sits in the middle, with a comma on each side, and then the main clause continues with its verb:

- *Der Film, den wir gestern gesehen haben, war langweilig.* — The film we saw yesterday was boring.
- *Die Werbung, die vor dem Video kommt, nervt mich.* — The ad that comes before the video annoys me. (*nerven* = to annoy, colloquial)

Notice "verb, comma, verb" in the middle: *haben, war* and *kommt, nervt*. The first verb ends the relative clause; the second is the verb of the main clause, which is still in position 2 (the whole subject *der Film, den …* counts as position 1).

## Preview: the dative forms

You will also meet relative pronouns in the dative, after verbs like *helfen* and *gefallen* (lesson 7) and after prepositions like *mit* and *bei*. Here, three forms are new: masculine and neuter *dem*, feminine *der*, and the plural *denen* (with an extra *-en*).

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dative | dem | der | dem | denen |

- *Das ist der Freund, dem ich mit dem Laptop geholfen habe.* — That's the friend I helped with the laptop.
- *Die Kollegin, mit der ich spreche, kommt aus Graz.* — The colleague I'm talking to is from Graz.
- *Das sind die Nachbarn, denen ich unser WLAN-Passwort gegeben habe.* — Those are the neighbours I gave our Wi-Fi password to.

With a preposition, the preposition comes first, before the relative pronoun: *der Bildschirm, auf dem* … (the screen on which …), never at the end as in English ("the screen I work on"). You only need to recognize these forms now; the reference sheet has the full table.

### alles, was

After *alles*, *etwas*, *nichts* and *das*, German uses *was* as the relative pronoun: *Das ist alles, was ich weiß.* — That's everything I know. *Gibt es etwas, was du nicht online kaufst?* — Is there anything you don't buy online?

## Defining words with relative clauses

When you don't know a word, describe it: *Das ist ein Ding, das man für den Computer braucht. Man schreibt damit.* (*die Tastatur*) The pattern *ein Ding / eine Person / ein Ort, der/die/das …* works for almost everything, in conversation and in the speaking exam.

## Dialogue: Oma gets a laptop

Lukas helps his grandmother with her new laptop.

> Oma: Lukas, kannst du mir mal helfen? Das ist der Laptop, den mir deine Mutter geschenkt hat. Aber der Bildschirm ist ganz schwarz.
>
> Lukas: Du musst ihn erst einschalten, Oma. Hier, die Taste, die oben rechts ist. So!
>
> Oma: Ah, jetzt sehe ich etwas. Und wie komme ich ins Internet?
>
> Lukas: Zuerst brauchst du das WLAN. Hast du den Zettel, den der Techniker dir gegeben hat? Da steht das Passwort.
>
> Oma: Ja, hier. Aber die Tastatur ist so klein! Ich finde die Buchstaben nicht.
>
> Lukas: Kein Problem, ich tippe es ein. So, jetzt bist du online. Was möchtest du machen?
>
> Oma: Ich möchte die Sendung über Italien sehen, die gestern Abend im Fernsehen kam. Ich war beim Arzt und habe sie verpasst.
>
> Lukas: Die findest du in der Mediathek. Das ist eine Webseite, auf der man alle Sendungen noch einmal sehen kann. Schau, hier ist sie.
>
> Oma: Wunderbar! Und kann ich sie speichern?
>
> Lukas: Du kannst sie herunterladen. Aber ich würde sie mir einfach online ansehen. Und, Oma: Bitte lösch nichts, was du nicht kennst!

Translation:

> Grandma: Lukas, can you help me? This is the laptop your mother gave me. But the screen is completely black.
>
> Lukas: You have to switch it on first, Grandma. Here, the key at the top right. There!
>
> Grandma: Ah, now I can see something. And how do I get on the internet?
>
> Lukas: First you need the Wi-Fi. Have you got the note the technician gave you? The password is on it.
>
> Grandma: Yes, here. But the keyboard is so small! I can't find the letters.
>
> Lukas: No problem, I'll type it in. There, now you're online. What would you like to do?
>
> Grandma: I'd like to watch the programme about Italy that was on TV last night. I was at the doctor's and missed it.
>
> Lukas: You'll find it in the Mediathek. That's a website where you can watch all the programmes again. Look, here it is.
>
> Grandma: Wonderful! And can I save it?
>
> Lukas: You can download it. But I'd just watch it online. And Grandma: please don't delete anything you don't know!

The relative pronouns: *den* (masculine accusative: the mother gave the laptop), *die oben rechts ist* (feminine nominative), *die gestern Abend … kam* (*die Sendung*, nominative), *auf der* (dative after a preposition) and *was* after *nichts*. Other words: *einschalten* = to switch on, *die Taste* = key (on a keyboard), *der Zettel* = note, slip of paper, *eintippen* = to type in, *verpassen* = to miss, *die Mediathek* = the online archive of a TV channel.

## Pronunciation

- *Tastatur* is stressed on the last syllable: tas-ta-TUR.
- *herunterladen*: he-RUN-ter-la-den. The stress is on *-run-*, not on *her-*.
- *Bildschirm*: BILD-schirm; the *sch* is like English "sh".
- *WLAN* is said "VAY-lahn"; Germans rarely say "Wi-Fi". *Video* is VI-de-o, *Internet* IN-ter-net.
- *Kommentar*: kom-men-TAR, stress at the end.

## Common mistakes

- Wrong gender from the wrong noun. In *die Frau, die das Video gemacht hat*, the pronoun agrees with *Frau*, not with *Video*.
- Taking the case from the main clause. *Ich kenne einen Mann, den in Wien wohnt* is wrong: the man lives in Vienna, so he is the subject: *der in Wien wohnt*.
- Verb not at the end: *der Film, den ich habe gesehen* → *den ich gesehen habe*.
- Splitting a separable verb: *die Sendung, die fängt um acht an* → *die um acht anfängt*.
- Forgetting the commas. German relative clauses always have them, on both sides if the sentence continues.
- *was* after a noun: *das Handy, was ich gekauft habe* is heard in casual speech but wrong in writing. Use *das*.
- Dropping the pronoun as in English: *der Film ich gesehen habe* → *der Film, den ich gesehen habe*.

## Key points

- A relative clause describes a noun (the antecedent). It starts with a relative pronoun, ends with the conjugated verb, and is set off by commas.
- Nominative and accusative relative pronouns = the definite article: *der, die, das, die*; only masculine accusative changes to *den*.
- Gender and number come from the antecedent; case comes from the pronoun's job inside the relative clause.
- Dative forms (preview): *dem, der, dem, denen*. After a preposition: *mit der, auf dem*.
- After *alles, etwas, nichts* use *was*.
- Media words: *herunterladen, hochladen, speichern, löschen, sich einloggen; die Sendung, die Nachrichten, die Werbung*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Holidays and celebrations
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Festivals are where a language meets a culture. In this lesson you learn the main holidays of the German-speaking countries, what people do on them and what they say to each other. On the grammar side there is nothing frightening, but several things come together: the **[[dative]]** in invitations and good wishes (*Ich gratuliere dir*, *Wir wünschen Ihnen …*), **[[ordinal numbers]]** in dates (*am vierundzwanzigsten Dezember*), *einer, keiner, meiner* used on their own as pronouns, and a review of *wann, wenn* and *als* (lesson 4) for telling stories about past holidays.

## The festive year

| when | holiday | what people do |
|---|---|---|
| December | der Advent | four Sundays before Christmas; a candle is lit each Sunday; children open a door of the *Adventskalender* each day from 1 December |
| 24 December | der Heiligabend | the tree (*der Weihnachtsbaum*) is decorated, the family eats together, presents are given in the evening |
| 25–26 December | Weihnachten | two public holidays: visiting relatives, big meals |
| 31 December | Silvester | parties, *Feuerwerk* at midnight, people toast with *Sekt* |
| 1 January | Neujahr | a public holiday; people sleep late |
| February / March | der Karneval, der Fasching | people dress up in costumes, parades in the streets |
| March / April | Ostern | painted eggs, chocolate bunnies, family lunch |

Some notes on the words:

- *Weihnachten, Ostern* and *Neujahr* are neuter, and *Silvester* is masculine or neuter, but all four are usually used without an article: *Weihnachten ist bald. Was machst du Silvester?* In good wishes, *Weihnachten* and *Ostern* behave like plurals: *Frohe Weihnachten! Frohe Ostern!* With a preposition, Germans say *an* or *zu*: *an Weihnachten* (more southern), *zu Ostern* (more northern). Both are correct.
- In Germany, presents are opened on the evening of *Heiligabend*, not on the morning of the 25th as in Britain or the USA.
- The same season has three names: *Karneval* in the Rhineland (Köln, Düsseldorf, Mainz), *Fasching* in Bavaria and Austria, *Fastnacht* (Swiss *Fasnacht*) in the south-west and Switzerland. People *verkleiden sich* (dress up) in a *Kostüm*.
- *der Feiertag* is a public holiday: shops are closed. Each country has a national day: in Germany 3 October, in Austria 26 October, in Switzerland 1 August. Some holidays exist only in some German states.
- *schmücken* means to decorate: *Wir schmücken den Weihnachtsbaum mit Kerzen und Sternen.* The decorations are *die Dekoration* (casually *die Deko*).
- *der Brauch* (plural *die Bräuche*) is a custom; *die Tradition* is a tradition. *Das ist bei uns Tradition* — that's a tradition in our family.
- Private celebrations: *die Feier* is a celebration or party (*die Geburtstagsfeier*, *die Hochzeitsfeier*); the host is *der Gastgeber* or *die Gastgeberin*. A *Torte* is a layered cream cake, fancier than a *Kuchen*.

### What to say

| situation | German | English |
|---|---|---|
| before Christmas | *Frohe Weihnachten!* | Merry Christmas! |
| before New Year | *Guten Rutsch!* / *Einen guten Rutsch ins neue Jahr!* | Happy New Year! (lit. "a good slide into the new year") |
| after midnight | *Frohes neues Jahr!* / *Prost Neujahr!* | Happy New Year! |
| Easter | *Frohe Ostern!* | Happy Easter! |
| raising a glass | *Prost!* / *Zum Wohl!* | Cheers! |
| birthday | *Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!* / *Herzlichen Glückwunsch!* | Happy birthday! |

*der Glückwunsch* (plural *die Glückwünsche*) is a congratulation or good wish: *Herzliche Glückwünsche zur Hochzeit!* *Guten Rutsch* is only said before 1 January. On the evening itself, people raise their glasses and *stoßen an* (*anstoßen*, to clink glasses): *Lasst uns auf das neue Jahr anstoßen!* — Let's drink to the new year! *anstoßen* is separable with a stem change: *er stößt an*, *hat angestoßen*.

## The dative in invitations and good wishes

Wishes, thanks and congratulations are full of dative objects, because they are things you give *to* someone (lesson 7). The person receiving is dative:

| verb | pattern | example |
|---|---|---|
| gratulieren | jemandem zu etwas | *Ich gratuliere dir zum Geburtstag.* — Happy birthday to you. |
| wünschen | jemandem etwas | *Wir wünschen Ihnen frohe Weihnachten.* — We wish you a merry Christmas. |
| danken | jemandem für etwas | *Ich danke euch für die schöne Feier.* — Thank you for the lovely party. |
| schenken | jemandem etwas | *Was schenkst du deiner Mutter?* — What are you giving your mother? |
| einladen | jemanden zu etwas | *Wir laden dich zu unserer Feier ein.* — We're inviting you to our party. |

Watch the cases. *gratulieren* takes only a dative person (*dir*, never *dich*), and the occasion goes with *zu* + dative: *zum Geburtstag, zur Hochzeit*. *einladen* is different: the guest is accusative (*dich*, *Sie*), and the event goes with *zu*: *Ich lade Sie zu meinem Geburtstag ein.*

A quick review of the dative pronouns: *mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen*.

And the dative after *zu, mit, bei, nach, seit, aus, von*: *mit meiner Familie*, *bei meinen Eltern*, *nach dem Essen*, *seit dem ersten Advent*.

## Dates with ordinal numbers

An ordinal number says the position in a row: first, second, third. You met them in A1 for dates (*am dritten Mai*). Here is the full rule:

- 1 to 19: number + *-te*: *der zweite, vierte, zehnte, neunzehnte*.
- From 20: number + *-ste*: *der zwanzigste, vierundzwanzigste, einunddreißigste*.
- Irregular: *der erste* (1st), *der dritte* (3rd), *der siebte* (7th), and *der achte* (only one *t*).

In writing, an ordinal is a number with a full stop: *der 24. Dezember*. The ending depends on the case, like any adjective after *der*:

| use | form | example |
|---|---|---|
| What's the date? | der …te | *Heute ist der vierundzwanzigste Dezember.* |
| On which day? | am …ten | *Am vierundzwanzigsten feiern wir.* |
| from … to … | vom …ten bis zum …ten | *Wir haben vom 23. bis zum 27. frei.* |
| at the top of a letter | den …ten | *Wien, den 3. Oktober 2026* |

Read *vom 23. bis zum 27.* aloud as *vom dreiundzwanzigsten bis zum siebenundzwanzigsten*.

## einer, keiner, meiner: ein-words as pronouns

When it's clear which noun you mean, you can drop the noun and use *ein*, *kein* or a possessive on its own. This kind of **[[indefinite pronoun]]** takes the ending that the noun's *der*-article would have, so the gender shows clearly:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative | einer / keiner / meiner | eine / keine / meine | eins / keins / meins | — / keine / meine |
| accusative | einen / keinen / meinen | eine / keine / meine | eins / keins / meins | — / keine / meine |

The difference from the article is in two places: the masculine nominative (*einer, keiner, meiner*, not *ein, kein, mein*) and the neuter nominative and accusative (*eins, keins, meins*, not *ein, kein, mein*).

- *Hast du schon einen Weihnachtsbaum? — Ja, wir haben gestern einen gekauft.* — Have you got a Christmas tree yet? — Yes, we bought one yesterday.
- *Brauchen wir noch Kerzen? — Nein, wir haben genug. Im Schrank liegen noch welche.* — Do we still need candles? — No, there are still some in the cupboard. (*welche* works as the plural of *einer/eine/eins*: some.)
- *Ist das dein Glas? — Nein, das ist nicht meins. Meins steht da drüben.* — Is that your glass? — No, it's not mine. Mine is over there.
- *Hat jemand ein Kostüm für mich? — Leider hat keiner eins.* — Has anyone got a costume for me? — Unfortunately, nobody has one. (*keiner* = nobody, no one.)

## Telling holiday stories: wann, wenn, als

These three all translate as "when", but they do different jobs (lesson 4):

- *wann* asks a question: *Wann feiert ihr Silvester?* Also in indirect questions: *Weißt du, wann die Party anfängt?*
- *als* is for one single event or period in the past: *Als ich zehn war, haben wir Weihnachten in Kanada gefeiert.*
- *wenn* is for things that happen again and again ("whenever"), and for the present and the future: *Wenn das Wetter an Ostern schön ist, suchen die Kinder die Eier im Garten. Wenn du kommst, backe ich eine Torte.*

A test: if you can say "whenever", or the time is now or later, use *wenn*. If it happened once in the past, *als*.

## Text: an invitation and an answer

> Liebe Clara, lieber Ben,
>
> am Samstag, dem 31. Dezember, feiern wir Silvester bei uns, und wir laden euch herzlich ein! Wir fangen um 20 Uhr mit einem Buffet an. Um Mitternacht gehen wir auf den Balkon, sehen das Feuerwerk an und stoßen zusammen an. Wer möchte, kann gern ein Kostüm tragen, weil das Motto „die Achtzigerjahre“ ist. Könnt ihr mir bis zum 20. Bescheid sagen? Dann kann ich genug Sekt kaufen.
>
> Viele Grüße und schöne Feiertage!
>
> Jana

Translation: Dear Clara, dear Ben, on Saturday the 31st of December we're celebrating New Year's Eve at our place, and you're warmly invited! We'll start at 8 pm with a buffet. At midnight we'll go out on the balcony, watch the fireworks and toast together. Anyone who likes can wear a costume, because the theme is "the eighties". Can you let me know by the 20th? Then I can buy enough sparkling wine. Best wishes and happy holidays! Jana

Note *am Samstag, dem 31. Dezember*: after *am*, the date that follows is dative too (*dem einunddreißigsten*). *Bescheid sagen* means to let someone know (lesson 23).

## Dialogue: at the party

> Jana: Da seid ihr ja! Schön, dass ihr gekommen seid. Clara, was für ein tolles Kostüm!
>
> Clara: Danke! Das habe ich auf dem Flohmarkt gefunden. Wir haben auch etwas für die Gastgeberin. Hier, bitte!
>
> Jana: Oh, eine Kerze und Pralinen! Vielen Dank, das wäre nicht nötig gewesen. Möchtet ihr etwas trinken?
>
> Ben: Gern. Hast du noch ein Glas für mich? Meins habe ich in der Küche stehen lassen.
>
> Jana: Hier ist eins. Sag mal, Ben, was macht ihr eigentlich normalerweise an Silvester?
>
> Ben: Als ich klein war, waren wir immer bei meiner Oma in den Bergen. Wenn es geschneit hat, sind wir um Mitternacht mit Fackeln durch den Wald gegangen. Das war unser Brauch.
>
> Clara: Und Feuerwerk gab es keins, weil die Oma Angst um ihre Tiere hatte!
>
> Jana: Hier gibt es leider eine Menge. Achtung, gleich ist es zwölf! Zehn, neun, acht …
>
> Alle: … drei, zwei, eins! Frohes neues Jahr! Prost!

Translation:

> Jana: There you are! How nice that you came. Clara, what a great costume!
>
> Clara: Thanks! I found it at the flea market. We've got something for the hostess too. Here you are!
>
> Jana: Oh, a candle and chocolates! Thank you so much, you shouldn't have. Would you like something to drink?
>
> Ben: Yes, please. Have you got another glass for me? I left mine in the kitchen.
>
> Jana: Here's one. Tell me, Ben, what do you usually do on New Year's Eve?
>
> Ben: When I was little we were always at my grandma's in the mountains. Whenever it snowed, we walked through the forest with torches at midnight. That was our custom.
>
> Clara: And there were no fireworks at all, because grandma was worried about her animals!
>
> Jana: Here there are lots, unfortunately. Look out, it's nearly twelve! Ten, nine, eight …
>
> All: … three, two, one! Happy New Year! Cheers!

Notice *meins* and *eins* (neuter, *das Glas*), *keins* (*das Feuerwerk*), *als ich klein war* (one period in the past) and *wenn es geschneit hat* (each time it snowed). New words: *der Flohmarkt* = flea market, *die Pralinen* = chocolates, *das wäre nicht nötig gewesen* = you shouldn't have, *die Fackel* = torch.

## Pronunciation

- *Weihnachten*: WEIH-nach-ten, with *ei* as in "eye" and the *ach*-sound.
- *Silvester*: sil-VES-ter, with a German *v* = "v" sound here, because the word is Latin.
- *Feuerwerk*: FEU-er-werk, *eu* like "oy".
- *Heiligabend*: hei-lig-A-bend; the *-ig* is said like *-ich*.
- *Dekoration*: de-ko-ra-TSION, stress at the end, *-tion* = "tsyohn".

## Common mistakes

- *Ich gratuliere dich* → *Ich gratuliere dir* (dative).
- *Ich lade dir ein* → *Ich lade dich ein* (accusative).
- *Frohe Weihnachten* to someone on 31 December: too late! Say *Guten Rutsch!*
- *der Weihnachten*, *die Ostern*: in Germany, use them without an article.
- *am vierundzwanzigste Dezember* → *am vierundzwanzigsten* (after *am*: *-ten*).
- *Ich habe kein* (as a full answer) → *Ich habe keinen / keine / keins*. The pronoun needs its ending.
- *Wenn ich ein Kind war, …* for one period in the past → *Als ich ein Kind war, …*

## Key points

- *Weihnachten, Ostern, Silvester, Neujahr*: normally no article (*Frohe Weihnachten!*); *an/zu Weihnachten*.
- *gratulieren* + dative + *zu*; *wünschen, danken, schenken* + dative person; *einladen* + accusative + *zu*.
- Ordinals: *-te* up to 19, *-ste* from 20; *erste, dritte, siebte, achte*. *am …ten, vom …ten bis zum …ten*.
- *einer, eine, eins* and *keiner, meiner* stand alone and show the gender: *Ich habe einen. Das ist meins.*
- *als* = once in the past; *wenn* = whenever, now, future; *wann* = question.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Writing SMS and e-mails: asking, apologizing, cancelling
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In A1 you learned the frame of a message: an opening, a few sentences, a closing. At A2 you are expected to do more with it: apologize, explain a problem, ask for something, move an appointment, confirm or cancel, and give reasons that are linked properly. These are everyday tasks (a message to a friend who is waiting, an e-mail to your teacher or landlord), and they are also exactly what the writing part of the Goethe-Zertifikat A2 asks for (lesson 24).

This lesson has three parts: choosing the right **[[register]]** (how formal to be), a toolbox of phrases for each kind of message, and a method for covering three points in 20 to 40 words without forgetting one.

## Register: du, Sie and the in-between

Register is the level of formality you choose for a reader. A message has three levels, not two:

| | who | address | opening | closing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| informal | friends, family, classmates | du / ihr | *Hallo Tim,* / *Hi Tim,* / *Liebe Sara, Lieber Tim,* | *Viele Grüße* / *Liebe Grüße* / *Bis bald!* |
| semi-formal | people you know but say *Sie* to: your teacher, a colleague, a neighbour, your landlord | Sie | *Liebe Frau Brandt,* / *Lieber Herr Yilmaz,* / *Hallo Frau Brandt,* | *Viele Grüße* / *Herzliche Grüße* / *Freundliche Grüße* |
| formal | offices, companies, people you don't know | Sie | *Sehr geehrte Frau Brandt,* / *Sehr geehrter Herr Yilmaz,* / *Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,* | *Mit freundlichen Grüßen* |

The semi-formal level is the one learners find tricky. Use *Sie*, but a warmer opening and closing: *Liebe Frau Brandt, … Viele Grüße*. *Sehr geehrte …* is correct too, but it sounds like a letter from a bank. The exam's e-mail task is usually semi-formal.

Rules that still apply from A1:

- *Liebe* + woman, *Lieber* + man; *Sehr geehrte Frau*, *Sehr geehrter Herr*. Always with the surname: *Liebe Frau Brandt*, not *Liebe Frau Anna*.
- A comma after the opening, then a small letter: *Liebe Frau Brandt, leider …*
- No comma after the closing, and your name on its own line.
- *Sie, Ihr, Ihnen* always have a capital letter. *du, dich, dein* can be written small or, in letters, with a capital (*Du, Dein*); both are correct, but be consistent.
- *herzlich* means warm, warmly: *Herzliche Grüße* (a closing between *Viele* and *Liebe* in warmth), *Herzlichen Dank!* (Many thanks!), *Sie sind herzlich eingeladen* (you are warmly invited).

### Short forms in text messages

In an SMS or chat, people shorten a lot: *LG* (*Liebe Grüße*), *VG* (*Viele Grüße*), *hdl* (*hab dich lieb*), *sorry* instead of *Entschuldigung*. They are fine between friends, but in the exam write the full forms.

## The toolbox

### Asking for something

| informal | semi-formal / formal |
|---|---|
| *Kannst du mir bitte … ?* | *Könnten Sie mir bitte … ?* |
| *Hast du Zeit, mir zu helfen?* | *Wäre es möglich, dass … ?* |
| *Weißt du, wann / ob … ?* | *Können Sie mir sagen, wann / ob … ?* |
| *Sag mir bitte Bescheid.* | *Bitte geben Sie mir Bescheid.* |

*Bescheid sagen* / *Bescheid geben* means to let someone know, and it is extremely common: *Sag mir Bescheid, wenn du da bist.* — Let me know when you're there. The polite forms with *könnten* and *wäre* are from lesson 15, and the indirect questions with *ob* from lesson 4.

For information from an office you ask for *eine Auskunft* (a piece of information): *Ich hätte gern eine Auskunft über die Kurse.* And you can ask for *eine Rückmeldung*, a reply or feedback: *Ich freue mich auf Ihre Rückmeldung.*

### Apologizing

- *Es tut mir leid, dass ich mich nicht gemeldet habe.* — I'm sorry I haven't been in touch.
- *Entschuldige bitte, dass ich so spät antworte.* (du) / *Entschuldigen Sie bitte, dass …* (Sie)
- *Ich verspäte mich leider.* — I'm running late, unfortunately.

*Es tut mir leid* (often just *Tut mir leid*) is followed by a *dass*-clause when you say what you're sorry for. *sich melden* means to get in touch, to call or write: *Melde dich, wenn du Zeit hast!* — Get in touch when you're free. *sich verspäten* is to be late: *Der Zug verspätet sich*; *Ich habe mich verspätet*.

### Cancelling, postponing, confirming

- *Leider muss ich unseren Termin absagen, weil …* — Unfortunately I have to cancel our appointment because …
- *Können wir das Treffen auf Donnerstag verschieben?* — Can we move the meeting to Thursday? (*verschieben* = to postpone; *hat verschoben*)
- *Ich sage gern zu.* / *Ich komme gern.* — I'm happy to accept. (*zusagen* is the opposite of *absagen*.)
- *Hiermit bestätige ich den Termin am 4. Mai.* — I hereby confirm the appointment on 4 May. Something written that confirms is *eine Bestätigung*.
- *Ich möchte Ihnen mitteilen, dass …* — I would like to inform you that … *mitteilen* (separable) is a formal "tell"; a written notice is *eine Mitteilung*. A little less formal: *Ich möchte Sie darüber informieren, dass …*

### Giving reasons and consequences

Join your ideas with the three kinds of linking words you know:

- *weil* (verb at the end, lesson 3): *Ich kann nicht kommen, weil ich arbeiten muss.*
- *deshalb* (position 1, then the verb, lesson 16): *Mein Auto ist kaputt. Deshalb komme ich mit dem Bus.*
- *trotzdem* (position 1, then the verb): *Ich bin krank. Trotzdem komme ich zur Prüfung.*
- *denn* (position zero, normal order, A1): *Ich komme später, denn der Bus hat Verspätung.*

One linked reason per message shows the examiner, and any reader, that you can build a real sentence.

### Times and dates

- *am Freitag, dem 14. März* (in letters you will also see *am Freitag, den 14. März*)
- *um halb acht* (7:30), *gegen 19 Uhr* (around 7 pm), *zwischen 10 und 12 Uhr*
- *bis Montag* (by Monday), *ab nächster Woche* (from next week), *in zwei Tagen*
- *rechtzeitig* — in good time: *Bitte sagen Sie rechtzeitig Bescheid.*
- *vorher* (before, beforehand) and *nachher* (afterwards, later): *Ich rufe dich vorher an. Wir können nachher noch essen gehen.*
- *inzwischen* — meanwhile, by now: *Inzwischen geht es mir besser.*
- *möglichst* — as … as possible: *möglichst bald* (as soon as possible), *möglichst früh*.
- *dringend* — urgent, urgently: *Ich brauche dringend deine Hilfe.*

## Three points in 20 to 40 words

Exam tasks, and many real situations, give you three things to say. The method:

1. Read the points and number them. Each needs at least one full sentence; a forgotten point loses more than a grammar mistake.
2. Choose the register from the person: a friend → *du*, informal; a teacher or neighbour → *Sie*, semi-formal.
3. Write one or two sentences per point, using one link (*weil, deshalb, trotzdem*) somewhere.
4. Frame it: opening, closing, name.
5. Check: verb second in main clauses, verb last after *weil* and *dass*, one form of address all the way through, nouns with capitals.

Opening, closing and name don't count as much as the content, but they belong to the task. Don't write far more than asked; a longer text has more room for mistakes.

## Model messages

### An informal SMS (30 words)

Points: you're late, say why, ask your friend to do something.

> Hallo Mia, es tut mir leid, ich verspäte mich um 20 Minuten, weil mein Bus nicht kommt. Kaufst du die Karten? Ich gebe dir das Geld nachher. Bis gleich! Tom

Translation: Hi Mia, I'm sorry, I'm going to be 20 minutes late because my bus isn't coming. Could you buy the tickets? I'll give you the money afterwards. See you soon! Tom

### A semi-formal e-mail (40 words)

Points: you can't come to the course, why, ask for the material.

> Liebe Frau Brandt,
>
> leider kann ich nächste Woche nicht zum Kurs kommen, weil ich für meine Firma nach Hamburg fahren muss. Könnten Sie mir bitte die Aufgaben per E-Mail schicken? Dann kann ich zu Hause lernen.
>
> Viele Grüße
>
> Sofia Rossi

Translation: Dear Ms Brandt, unfortunately I can't come to the course next week, because I have to go to Hamburg for my company. Could you please send me the exercises by e-mail? Then I can study at home. Best wishes, Sofia Rossi

### A formal e-mail: moving an appointment

> Betreff: Termin am 12. Juni – Bitte um Verschiebung
>
> Sehr geehrter Herr Wagner,
>
> wir haben am Donnerstag, dem 12. Juni, um 9 Uhr einen Termin für die Reparatur der Heizung. Leider bin ich an diesem Tag nicht zu Hause. Könnten wir den Termin möglichst auf die nächste Woche verschieben? Ich bin jeden Tag ab 15 Uhr erreichbar. Im Anhang finden Sie ein Foto von der Heizung.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
>
> Anna Lindqvist

Translation: Subject: Appointment on 12 June – request to reschedule. Dear Mr Wagner, we have an appointment for the repair of the heating on Thursday, 12 June, at 9 am. Unfortunately I won't be at home that day. Could we move the appointment to next week if possible? I can be reached every day from 3 pm. Please find a photo of the heating attached. Yours sincerely, Anna Lindqvist

E-mail words: *der Betreff* is the subject line; *der Anhang* the attachment (*im Anhang* — attached); *weiterleiten* is to forward (*Ich leite dir die Mail weiter*); *erreichbar* means reachable, available by phone.

## Dialogue: a message thread

Ella and her flatmate Jonas write to each other during the day.

> Jonas: Hey, hast du die Mail vom Vermieter gesehen? Ich habe sie dir gerade weitergeleitet. Morgen kommt jemand wegen der Heizung, zwischen 8 und 12 Uhr.
>
> Ella: Oh nein, morgen früh habe ich eine Prüfung! Kannst du zu Hause bleiben?
>
> Jonas: Leider nicht, ich muss um 9 bei der Arbeit sein. Aber ich kann vorher den Schlüssel bei Frau Koch lassen.
>
> Ella: Super Idee. Sagst du ihr Bescheid? Und schreib bitte dem Vermieter, dass sie den Schlüssel hat.
>
> Jonas: Mach ich. Ich habe inzwischen auch eine Bestätigung bekommen: Der Techniker kommt um 10.
>
> Ella: Perfekt. Danke dir! Ich melde mich nachher, wenn ich mit der Prüfung fertig bin. Drück mir die Daumen!
>
> Jonas: Mach ich! Viel Erfolg! LG

Translation:

> Jonas: Hey, have you seen the e-mail from the landlord? I've just forwarded it to you. Tomorrow someone's coming about the heating, between 8 and 12.
>
> Ella: Oh no, I have an exam tomorrow morning! Can you stay at home?
>
> Jonas: Unfortunately not, I have to be at work at 9. But I can leave the key with Mrs Koch beforehand.
>
> Ella: Great idea. Will you let her know? And please write to the landlord that she has the key.
>
> Jonas: Will do. Meanwhile I've also got a confirmation: the technician is coming at 10.
>
> Ella: Perfect. Thanks! I'll get in touch afterwards, when I'm done with the exam. Keep your fingers crossed for me!
>
> Jonas: Will do! Good luck! Love, J.

*Drück mir die Daumen* is literally "press your thumbs for me": the German way to keep your fingers crossed. *Mach ich* is a casual "will do".

## Pronunciation

- *Grüße* has a long *ü*: GRÜ-ße. *Mit freundlichen Grüßen*: the *eu* is "oy".
- *geehrte*: ge-EHR-te, two separate *e* sounds.
- *bestätigen*: be-STÄ-ti-gen; *verschieben*: ver-SCHIE-ben, with a long *ie*.
- *Bescheid*: be-SCHEID, rhymes with *Zeit*.

## Common mistakes

- Mixing registers: *Liebe Frau Brandt, kannst du …* Pick *Sie* and keep it: *können Sie …*
- *Lieber Frau Brandt* / *Sehr geehrte Herr Wagner*. Match the ending to the person: *Liebe Frau*, *Sehr geehrter Herr*.
- A capital letter after the opening comma: *Liebe Mia, Es tut mir leid* → *es tut mir leid*.
- Missing a content point. Count your points before you finish.
- *Ich verspäte* without *mich*. It's reflexive: *Ich verspäte mich.*
- *Es tut mir leid, dass ich habe nicht geantwortet* → *dass ich nicht geantwortet habe* (verb at the end).
- *Deshalb ich komme später* → *Deshalb komme ich später.*
- Writing *sie* or *ihnen* small when you mean "you": *Können Sie mir helfen? Ich danke Ihnen.*

## Key points

- Three registers: informal (*du*, *Liebe/Hallo …*, *Viele/Liebe Grüße*), semi-formal (*Sie*, *Liebe Frau …*, *Viele/Herzliche Grüße*), formal (*Sie*, *Sehr geehrte/r …*, *Mit freundlichen Grüßen*).
- Asking: *Kannst du / Könnten Sie …?*; apologizing: *Es tut mir leid, dass …*; cancelling and moving: *absagen, verschieben*; confirming: *bestätigen, zusagen*; *Bescheid sagen* = let someone know.
- Link reasons with *weil*, *deshalb* or *trotzdem*.
- Cover every content point; check verb positions and capitals at the end.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The Goethe-Zertifikat A2 and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last lesson of German A2. Like the last lesson of A1, it does three things: it explains what A2 means, describes the best-known exam at this level, the Goethe-Zertifikat A2, with strategies for each part, and reviews the grammar of the whole course with pointers back to the lessons. The questions at the end cover the whole course, so use them as a final check. You don't have to take the exam, but the free official practice tests are the best way to find out whether you have really reached A2.

## What A2 means

A2 is the second level of the **[[CEFR]]**, the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. In plain words, someone at A2:

- can follow short, clear sentences about the everyday things that matter to them: family, shopping, home, work, the local area;
- can get through simple everyday situations where people swap information directly: buying, booking, arranging a time, asking the way;
- can say in simple words where they come from, what their life is like and what they need.

The biggest difference (*der Unterschied*) from A1: you no longer depend on the other person speaking slowly and helping all the time. You can tell a short story in the past (lessons 1–2), give reasons and opinions (lesson 3), describe people and things in detail (lessons 8–12), and handle shops, offices, doctors and messages (lessons 10–11 and 17–23). Conversations on unfamiliar or abstract topics are still hard, and that is normal: that is B1.

## The Goethe-Zertifikat A2

The adult version of the exam has four parts. Lesen, Hören and Schreiben are taken in writing, one after the other; Sprechen is a separate oral exam, usually taken in pairs.

| part | time | parts | what you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lesen (reading) | 30 minutes | 4 | a short newspaper or magazine text; an information board (for example in a building or a shop); a personal e-mail; matching people to small ads |
| Hören (listening) | about 30 minutes | 4 | short announcements, radio items and phone messages; a conversation whose details you match to pictures; short everyday conversations; a radio interview |
| Schreiben (writing) | 30 minutes | 2 | an informal SMS of 20–30 words; a semi-formal e-mail of 30–40 words; each covers three content points |
| Sprechen (speaking) | about 15 minutes | 3 | in pairs, with no preparation time: asking and answering questions with word cards; talking about your own life; planning an appointment together |

There are 100 points: 75 for the written parts and 25 for speaking. To pass you need 60 points overall, and at least 45 of the 75 written points and 15 of the 25 speaking points. The grades:

| points | grade |
|---|---|
| 90–100 | sehr gut (very good) |
| 80–89 | gut (good) |
| 70–79 | befriedigend (satisfactory) |
| 60–69 | ausreichend (sufficient, a pass) |

The Goethe-Institut offers free official practice material: a complete model test with audio and answers, a second practice test, and an interactive online version.

- [Model test for adults (Modellsatz, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/materialien/A2/A2_Modellsatz_Erwachsene.pdf)
- [Practice test for adults (Übungssatz, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/materialien/A2/A2_Uebungssatz_Erwachsene.pdf)
- [Interactive online practice](https://bfu.goethe.de/a2_mod_2MX5/)
- [Official exam rules (Durchführungsbestimmungen, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/resources/files/pdf325/durchfuehrungsbestimmungen_a2.pdf)

Dates, fees and details can change, so check with the exam centre where you register. Other A2 exams (telc, ÖSD) test the same level, though the tasks are a little different (*unterschiedlich*).

## Strategies for each part

### Lesen

- Read the task and the questions first, then the text. You are looking for specific information, not translating every word.
- In matching tasks (people and ads), underline the key need of each person: a time, a price, an age, a place. Then look for an ad that fits all of it, not just one word. Watch out: one person may have no matching ad.
- If you don't know the meaning (*die Bedeutung*) of a word, guess it from the context and move on.
- Information boards are lists of floors, departments or offices: scan, don't read. The vocabulary of lessons 10, 14 and 19 helps.
- Read the small words carefully (*genau lesen*): *nur, nicht, kein, schon, noch nicht, erst*. They often decide the answer. A *Hinweis* (note) in small print may be important too.

### Hören

- Before each audio, read the questions and think about which words you will hear: a time? a place? a price?
- In announcements (*Durchsagen* at the station, *Ansagen* on the phone), listen for numbers: platforms, times, phone numbers. Note them on paper while you listen.
- People often correct themselves: *Wir treffen uns um sieben, nein, um halb acht.* The last information counts.
- Don't be put off by one word you missed. Keep listening; the answer often comes a moment later.

### Schreiben

- Lesson 23 is your preparation. Number the three points and write at least one sentence for each.
- Choose the register from the person: a friend → *du*, informal; a teacher, colleague or neighbour → *Sie*, semi-formal.
- Use one or two linking words (*weil, deshalb, trotzdem, dass*) and a polite form (*Könnten Sie …? Ich würde gern …*).
- Keep to the length. A few words more are fine; double the length means double the room for mistakes.
- Save three minutes at the end to check verb positions, capitals and endings.

### Sprechen

- The speaking test is a conversation (*ein Gespräch*), and the examiners want to see that you can react to your partner, not just recite.
- Questions with word cards: you get a topic and a word, and you make a question. Make it simple and complete: topic *Freizeit*, word *Wochenende* → *Was machst du am Wochenende?* Then answer your partner's question with two or three sentences, not one word.
- Talking about your life: you get a card with a question about your everyday life (*Wohnen, Essen, Reisen, Arbeit* …). Prepare at home: for each common topic, have four or five sentences ready, including the past (*Letztes Jahr bin ich …*), a reason (*weil …*) and an opinion (*Ich finde, dass …*).
- Planning together: you and your partner each have a calendar with appointments and must find a time for something you want to do together. Suggest, react, and agree. The phrases are below.
- If you don't understand: *Wie bitte? Kannst du das noch einmal sagen? Was bedeutet …?* Asking is part of the conversation; silence is not.

### Planning an appointment: phrases

| suggesting | reacting | agreeing |
|---|---|---|
| *Hast du am Samstag Zeit?* | *Am Samstag passt es mir leider nicht.* | *Gut, dann machen wir das so.* |
| *Wie wäre es mit Sonntag um zehn?* | *Da kann ich leider nicht, da habe ich …* | *Einverstanden!* |
| *Wollen wir uns nach dem Kurs treffen?* | *Um zehn ist es mir zu früh. Geht es auch später?* | *Super, das passt.* |
| *Sollen wir zusammen ein Geschenk kaufen?* | *Gute Idee! Aber wann?* | *Also treffen wir uns um drei am Bahnhof.* |

*Einverstanden* means "agreed, OK". *vereinbaren* is to arrange or agree on (*einen Termin vereinbaren*), and *der Zeitpunkt* is the point in time: *Ist das ein guter Zeitpunkt?*

## Exam language

Instructions are in German. These words come up often:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| die Anzeige | small ad, advertisement |
| die Durchsage / die Ansage | announcement (loudspeaker / recorded) |
| der Hinweis | note, tip, notice |
| das Thema | topic |
| beachten | to pay attention to, to note |
| verwechseln | to mix up, to confuse |
| zusammenfassen, die Zusammenfassung | to summarize, summary |
| die Lücke | gap (in a text) |
| die Reihenfolge | order, sequence |
| passend | suitable, matching |
| korrigieren | to correct |

- *Beachten Sie die Uhrzeit.* — Pay attention to the time.
- *Verwechseln Sie nicht Montag und Mittwoch!* — Don't mix up Monday and Wednesday!
- *Finden Sie die passende Anzeige.* — Find the matching ad.
- *Wann bekomme ich mein Ergebnis?* — When will I get my result?

## Review of the course

| reflexive verbs | *Ich freue mich. Ich wasche mir die Hände.* | 5 |

| adjective endings | *ein neuer Laptop, der neue Laptop, neuer Laptop* | 9, 10, 11 |
| comparison | *größer als, so groß wie, am größten* | 12 |
| two-way prepositions | *Wo? im Regal (dative). Wohin? ins Regal (accusative).* | 13 |
| time prepositions | *vor einem Jahr, seit zwei Wochen, ab Montag* | 14, 20 |
| Konjunktiv II | *Ich hätte gern … Könnten Sie …? Du solltest …* | 15 |
| linking adverbs | *deshalb, trotzdem, sonst*: verb right after | 16 |

| possession | *Annas Buch, das Auto von meinem Bruder* | 18 |
| lassen, indirect questions | *Ich lasse das Auto reparieren. Wissen Sie, wo …?* | 19 |

If you remember only three things from A2, make them these: in a subordinate clause, the verb goes to the end; adjective endings show gender and case when the article doesn't; and polite German lives in *würde, hätte, könnte*.

## Dialogue: planning together

Two learners, Marta and Dev, practise the third speaking task. They want to visit their friend Paula, who is in hospital.

> Marta: Dev, wir wollen Paula im Krankenhaus besuchen. Wann hast du Zeit?
>
> Dev: Hm, ich schaue mal in meinen Kalender. Am Montag arbeite ich bis 18 Uhr. Wie wäre es mit Dienstagvormittag?
>
> Marta: Da kann ich leider nicht, da habe ich um zehn einen Termin beim Zahnarzt. Geht es bei dir am Dienstagnachmittag?
>
> Dev: Nachmittags habe ich meinen Deutschkurs, der dauert bis vier. Aber danach habe ich frei.
>
> Marta: Gut, um halb fünf passt es mir auch. Und wir sollten vorher ein Geschenk kaufen. Was meinst du, Blumen?
>
> Dev: Ich glaube, Blumen sind im Krankenhaus nicht so praktisch. Wir könnten ihr eine Zeitschrift kaufen, die sie gern liest.
>
> Marta: Gute Idee! Ich kenne eine, die sie toll findet. Also: Wir treffen uns am Dienstag um halb fünf am Kiosk vor dem Krankenhaus?
>
> Dev: Einverstanden. Aber nicht verwechseln: der Kiosk am Haupteingang, nicht der am Parkplatz!

Translation:

> Marta: Dev, we want to visit Paula in hospital. When are you free?
>
> Dev: Hm, let me look in my calendar. On Monday I'm working until 6 pm. How about Tuesday morning?
>
> Marta: I'm afraid I can't then, I've got a dentist's appointment at ten. Does Tuesday afternoon work for you?
>
> Dev: In the afternoon I have my German course, which lasts until four. But after that I'm free.
>
> Marta: Good, half past four suits me too. And we should buy a present first. What do you think, flowers?
>
> Dev: I don't think flowers are very practical in hospital. We could buy her a magazine she likes reading.
>
> Marta: Good idea! I know one she thinks is great. So: we'll meet on Tuesday at half past four at the kiosk in front of the hospital?
>
> Dev: Agreed. But don't mix them up: the kiosk at the main entrance, not the one at the car park!

The dialogue uses a suggestion (*Wie wäre es mit …?*), a refusal with a reason, *sollten* and *könnten*, a relative clause (*eine Zeitschrift, die sie gern liest*; *der dauert bis vier* is spoken style) and the pronoun *eine*. Dev's last line avoids a *Missverständnis* (misunderstanding).

## Pronunciation

- *Missverständnis*: MISS-ver-ständ-nis, stress on the first syllable.
- *Thema*: TEH-ma; the *th* is a plain *t*.
- *Zusammenfassung*: zu-SAM-men-fas-sung.
- *korrigieren*: kor-ri-GIE-ren, stress on *-gie-*, like all *-ieren* verbs.

## Common mistakes

- Answering a card with one word. *Wochenende? — Fußball.* Say a full sentence and add a detail: *Am Wochenende spiele ich meistens Fußball, weil …*
- Ignoring your partner in the planning task. React to what they say: *Ah, am Montag arbeitest du. Und am Dienstag?*
- In Schreiben, writing *du* to a teacher, or forgetting the opening and closing.
- Thinking 45 written points are enough. You also need 15 in Sprechen, and 60 overall.
- *Ich habe eine Missverständnis* → *ein Missverständnis* (neuter).

## What comes next: B1

At B1 you will talk about experiences, plans and opinions in more detail and follow the main points of clear speech on familiar topics. The grammar adds the simple past of all verbs, the passive and the genitive in full. The Goethe-Zertifikat B1 is a common requirement for work, study and citizenship in Germany.

Until then, keep your vocabulary reviews going every day, read graded readers from the reading list, and find German you enjoy: podcasts for learners, series with German subtitles, a tandem partner.

## Key points

- A2: you handle routine everyday situations and simple exchanges about familiar things, and describe your background and needs.
- Goethe A2: Lesen 30 min, Hören about 30 min, Schreiben 30 min (SMS 20–30 words, e-mail 30–40 words), Sprechen about 15 min in pairs. Pass with 60/100 and at least 45/75 written and 15/25 speaking.
- Practise with the free official model test, practice test and interactive version.
- Planning: *Hast du … Zeit? Wie wäre es mit …? Da kann ich leider nicht. Einverstanden!*
- Exam language: *die Anzeige, die Durchsage, der Hinweis, die Lücke, beachten, verwechseln, passend*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson. Herzlichen Glückwunsch: you have finished German A2!

sections.name: Media, celebrations and the A2 exam

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich ___ in einem kleinen Dorf aufgewachsen."
questions.explanation: aufwachsen (to grow up) is a change of state, so it takes sein: Ich bin aufgewachsen. "habe" is the usual guess, but verbs like aufwachsen, sterben and werden use sein.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of "verstehen"?
questions.explanation: ver- is an inseparable prefix, so there is no ge-. Build it like stehen → gestanden, then drop the ge-: verstanden. "geverstanden" adds a ge- that inseparable verbs never take.

questions.stem: Complete: "Sie hat in Graz Medizin ___."
questions.explanation: Verbs ending in -ieren take no ge- in the participle: studieren → studiert. "gestudiert" is the most common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete: "Meine Eltern haben mich nach meinem Großvater ___."
questions.explanation: nennen is a mixed verb: the vowel changes to a and the participle ends in -t, like kennen → gekannt. So: genannt. "genennt" forgets the vowel change.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: German puts a year on its own, with no "in" (or with "im Jahr"). The year is position 1, so the verb follows: 2015 habe ich geheiratet. heiraten takes haben, not sein.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Großvater ___ letztes Jahr gestorben."
questions.explanation: sterben (to die) is a change of state, so it takes sein: Er ist gestorben. "hat gestorben" is wrong.

questions.stem: Which verb has NO ge- in its past participle?
questions.explanation: er- is an inseparable prefix, so erleben → erlebt. The others all have ge-: aufgewachsen and umgezogen (separable, -ge- in the middle) and geheiratet (heiraten has no prefix at all).

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe erst mit 30 Auto fahren gelernt" mean?
choices: I didn't learn to drive until I was 30.
I learned to drive first, at 30.
I learned to drive at 30 at the earliest.
I first learned to drive 30 years ago.
questions.explanation: erst + a time means "only then, not until then": something happened later than you might expect. It does not mean "first" (that's zuerst).

questions.stem: Read: "Paula ist 1979 in Bremen geboren. Nach dem Abitur hat sie eine Ausbildung als Köchin gemacht. 2005 hat sie ein eigenes Restaurant gegründet. Seit 2021 ist sie in Rente." What is Paula doing now?
choices: She is training to be a cook.
questions.explanation: in Rente sein means to be retired, and seit 2021 tells you it is still true today. The training and the restaurant (gegründet = founded) were earlier stages of her life.

questions.stem: A friend asks: "Wo bist du aufgewachsen?" Which answer fits?
choices: In Hamburg, aber mit 18 bin ich nach München gezogen.
questions.explanation: The question is where you grew up, so you name a place. "Ich habe in Hamburg aufgewachsen" uses the wrong auxiliary (bin aufgewachsen), and the other two answer different questions (how tall, how long).

questions.stem: Which word fits? "Die Reise nach Island war ein tolles ___."
questions.explanation: das Erlebnis is one memorable event you experience, and it is neuter, which fits "ein tolles". die Erfahrung is experience you gain over time, and it is feminine, so it would need "eine tolle".

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Nach dem Abschluss habe ich meine Heimat verlassen und bin nach Wien gegangt."
questions.explanation: gehen is a strong verb: the participle is gegangen, not "gegangt". verlassen is correct: an inseparable verb whose participle looks like the infinitive.

questions.stem: Complete: "Als Kind ___ ich jeden Tag um sieben Uhr aufstehen."
questions.explanation: The simple past of müssen drops the umlaut and adds -te: ich musste. The ich form has no extra ending, so "musstet" (the ihr form) is wrong, and "müsste" is a different form meaning "would have to".

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir ___ abends nicht fernsehen." (we weren't allowed to)
questions.explanation: dürfen → drop the umlaut, add -te: durfte; with wir: durften. "dürften" keeps the umlaut, which makes it a different form (lesson 15).

questions.stem: How do you say "I wanted a bike" in German?
questions.explanation: möchten has no past form of its own, so for "wanted" you use the past of wollen: ich wollte. "Ich mochte ein Fahrrad" means "I liked a bike".

questions.stem: Complete: "Du ___ damals sehr frech."
questions.explanation: The du form of the simple past adds -st: du warst. "war" is the ich and er/sie/es form, and "wart" is the ihr form.

questions.stem: Which infinitive belongs to "sie ging"?
questions.explanation: ging is the simple past of gehen (to go): a strong verb with a new vowel and no ending. The simple past of geben is gab.

questions.stem: In a normal conversation, which sentence sounds most natural?
choices: Gestern besuchte ich Oma, und wir aßen Kuchen.
Gestern habe ich Oma besucht, und wir haben Kuchen gegessen.
questions.explanation: In speech Germans use the perfect for most verbs: habe besucht, haben gegessen. The simple past "besuchte … aßen" is correct but sounds like a book. The first option breaks verb-second order, and besuchen takes haben.

questions.stem: What does "Damals gab es kein Internet" mean?
choices: Back then he didn't give us internet.
Back then there was no internet.
Back then the internet didn't work.
Back then we gave up the internet.
questions.explanation: gab is the simple past of geben, and es gab is the past of es gibt: "there was / there were". It's one of the most common simple past forms.

questions.stem: Read: "In der Grundschule hatte ich eine strenge Lehrerin. In der Pause durften wir nicht auf die Bäume klettern, und wer frech war, musste in der Klasse bleiben." What was NOT allowed?
questions.explanation: durften nicht klettern = were not allowed to climb. Children who were cheeky (frech) had to stay in the classroom, but the text only names climbing trees as forbidden.

questions.stem: In Germany, what does the grade 1 on a Zeugnis mean?
questions.explanation: German school grades go from 1 (sehr gut) to 6 (ungenügend), so 1 is the best. Many English speakers expect the opposite.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Mit sechs Jahren konntet ich schon lesen, aber ich mochte keine Märchen."
questions.explanation: The ich form of a modal in the simple past has no ending after -te: ich konnte. "konntet" is the ihr form. mochte is correct (the past of mögen).

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I remember my first teacher"?
choices: Ich erinnere mich meine erste Lehrerin.
Ich erinnere mich an meine erste Lehrerin.
Ich bin erinnert an meine erste Lehrerin.
questions.explanation: The chunk is sich erinnern an + accusative: Ich erinnere mich an … You need both the mich and the an.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mozart ___ 1756 in Salzburg geboren."
questions.explanation: For people who have died, Germans say wurde … geboren, using the simple past of werden. "ist geboren" is for living people (Ich bin 1990 geboren), and "wird" is present tense.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Wien arbeiten will.
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich will in Wien arbeiten.
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil will ich in Wien arbeiten.
Ich lerne Deutsch weil ich in Wien will arbeiten.
questions.explanation: weil sends the conjugated verb to the end, so the modal will comes last, after the infinitive: weil ich in Wien arbeiten will. And there is always a comma before weil.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich bin müde, weil ich jeden Tag um fünf Uhr ___."
questions.explanation: In a subordinate clause the separable verb moves to the end and joins its prefix again, written as one word: aufstehe. "stehe auf" is main-clause order.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich bin enttäuscht, weil du nicht ___."
questions.explanation: In the perfect, the auxiliary comes last of all in a subordinate clause, after the participle: angerufen hast.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Weil es regnet, ich nehme den Bus.
Weil regnet es, nehme ich den Bus.
Weil es regnet nehme den Bus ich.
Weil es regnet, nehme ich den Bus.
questions.explanation: When the weil clause comes first, it fills position 1, so the main verb follows straight after the comma: verb, comma, verb (regnet, nehme). "ich nehme" after the comma is English word order.

questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT correct?
choices: Ich glaube, dass er krank ist.
Ich glaube, dass er ist krank.
Ich glaube, er ist heute krank.
questions.explanation: You can use dass with the verb at the end, or leave dass out and use main-clause order. You can't mix them: "dass er ist krank" keeps the verb in the wrong place.

questions.stem: Complete: "Es ist wichtig, ___ du pünktlich bist."
questions.explanation: After "Es ist wichtig" you need the conjunction dass (double s), and the verb bist is at the end. "das" is the article or pronoun; "denn" would need the verb in position 2.

questions.stem: Which word completes BOTH gaps? "Ich bleibe heute zu Hause, ___ ich bin krank." / "Ich gehe nicht mit, ___ ich habe keine Zeit."
questions.explanation: The verb comes right after the subject (ich bin, ich habe), which is main-clause order, so the word must be denn. weil would need the verb at the end: weil ich krank bin.

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Ich finde, der Film war viel zu lang." You agree. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Da hast du recht = You're right there. recht haben uses haben, so "Ich bin recht" is wrong. "Das stimmt nicht" disagrees, and "Das ist mir egal" means you don't care.

questions.stem: What does "Ich bin stolz auf meine Tochter" mean?
questions.explanation: stolz auf = proud of. Worried would be "Ich mache mir Sorgen um …", furious is wütend and disappointed is enttäuscht.

questions.stem: Read: "Lina wollte am Samstag mit Ben ins Konzert gehen. Aber Ben hat die Karten vergessen, und das Konzert war ausverkauft." How does Lina probably feel?
questions.explanation: Ben forgot the tickets and the concert was sold out (ausverkauft), so Lina missed it: she is disappointed (enttäuscht). The other words are positive feelings.

questions.stem: Complete: "Meiner Meinung nach ___ das Hotel zu teuer."
questions.explanation: "Meiner Meinung nach" fills position 1, so the verb follows at once and then the subject: Meiner Meinung nach ist das Hotel zu teuer.

questions.stem: A friend asks: "Warum hast du so schlechte Laune?" Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation: A weil clause can answer a warum question on its own, with the auxiliary at the end: weil ich schlecht geschlafen habe. denn can't stand alone as an answer, and "hast" is the du form. (schlechte Laune = a bad mood)

questions.stem: Complete: "___ ich ein Kind war, hatte ich einen Hund."
questions.explanation: "When I was a child" is one period in the past, so German uses als. wenn is for repeated events or the future, and wann only asks questions.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ ich meine Oma besucht habe, gab es immer Kuchen."
questions.explanation: "immer" shows that it happened every time, again and again. For repeated events in the past, use wenn (whenever). als is only for one single occasion.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich weiß nicht, ___ er morgen kommt." (whether)
questions.explanation: "whether" fits in English, so German needs ob. English often says "if" here, which makes "wenn" tempting, but wenn is only for conditions and time.

questions.stem: Which question is correct?
choices: Können Sie mir sagen, wo ist der Bahnhof?
Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof?
Können Sie mir sagen, der Bahnhof wo ist?
questions.explanation: In an indirect question the question word stays at the front of the clause and the verb goes to the end: wo der Bahnhof ist. "wo ist der Bahnhof" keeps direct-question order.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Wenn das Wetter schön ist, gehen wir schwimmen.
Wenn das Wetter ist schön, gehen wir schwimmen.
Wenn das Wetter schön ist, wir gehen schwimmen.
Wann das Wetter schön ist, gehen wir schwimmen.
questions.explanation: The wenn clause has its verb at the end (schön ist), and the main clause starts with the verb: verb, comma, verb. wann is only a question word.

questions.stem: Turn into an indirect question: "Wann fängt der Kurs an?" → "Weißt du, ___?"
questions.explanation: Keep the question word wann, send the verb to the end and join the separable verb back together: wann der Kurs anfängt. "wenn" is not a question word.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Wann ich nach Hause komme, koche ich immer zuerst einen Tee."
questions.explanation: wann is only for questions. For "when(ever)" in a statement about something that happens again and again, use wenn: Wenn ich nach Hause komme, …

questions.stem: A colleague asks: "Was hast du am Wochenende vor?" What is she asking?
choices: What did you do at the weekend?
What are you doing at the weekend?
Do you have time before the weekend?
What do you have in front of you?
questions.explanation: vorhaben (separable: hast … vor) means to plan or intend, so she is asking about your plans. It's the normal way to ask what someone is doing later.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo Tim, ich weiß noch nicht, ob ich am Freitag kommen kann. Falls es klappt, bringe ich einen Salat mit. Ich sage dir morgen Bescheid. Mia" What do we know?
choices: Mia is definitely coming on Friday.
Mia isn't coming, but she will send a salad.
Mia doesn't know yet whether she can come.
Mia wants Tim to bring a salad.
questions.explanation: "ob ich am Freitag kommen kann" = whether I can come on Friday, so it's not decided. falls es klappt = in case it works out; only then will she bring a salad. (Bescheid sagen = to let someone know)

questions.stem: Complete: "___ wir in Rom ankamen, hat es geregnet."
questions.explanation: This is one occasion in the past (the day we arrived in Rome), so it's als. wenn would mean "whenever we arrived", which doesn't fit one trip.

questions.stem: Your friend is nervous about an exam. What do you say to encourage her?
questions.explanation: Das schaffst du! = You can do it! (schaffen = to manage). "Hat es geklappt?" asks afterwards whether it worked out, and the other two are discouraging.

questions.stem: Which word fits? "Das Museum ist am Montag geschlossen. Wir müssen unseren Plan ein bisschen ___: Wir gehen am Dienstag hin."
questions.explanation: ändern = to change something, to make it different. wechseln is for swapping one thing for another (die Stelle wechseln), erreichen means to reach, and aufgeben means to give up the plan completely, but here the plan only moves by a day.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich ziehe ___ schnell an."
questions.explanation: sich anziehen (to get dressed) is reflexive, and with ich the accusative reflexive pronoun is mich. There is no other object in the sentence, so it is not the dative mir. sich is only for er, sie, es, sie (plural) and Sie.

questions.stem: Complete: "Er rasiert ___ jeden Morgen."
questions.explanation: When he shaves himself, the pronoun points back to the subject, so it is the reflexive pronoun sich. "Er rasiert ihn" would mean he shaves someone else.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich putze ___ die Zähne."
questions.explanation: The sentence already has an accusative object (die Zähne), so the reflexive pronoun moves to the dative: mir. "mich" is the form without another object (Ich wasche mich). German uses the article with body parts, not a possessive.
