questions.stem: Complete: "Wir haben ___ im Urlaub gut erholt."
questions.explanation: The reflexive pronoun for wir is uns, in both accusative and dative. sich is only for third person and Sie, so "Wir haben sich erholt" is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Reflexive verbs always form the perfect with haben, the pronoun stays right after haben, and the participle goes to the end. There is no other object, so the pronoun is the accusative mich, not mir.

questions.stem: What does "Ich langweile mich." mean?
questions.explanation: sich langweilen means to be bored. "I'm boring" would be "Ich bin langweilig", which describes you, not how you feel. Annoyed is "Ich ärgere mich"; tired is "Ich bin müde".

questions.stem: What does "Nach der Arbeit ziehe ich mich um." mean?
choices: After work I go for a walk.
questions.explanation: With sich, umziehen means to get changed (put on different clothes). Without sich it means to move house: "Wir ziehen nach Berlin um." To get undressed is sich ausziehen.

questions.stem: Read: "Lukas steht um sieben auf. Er duscht, rasiert sich und zieht sich an. Dann trinkt er schnell einen Kaffee, weil er sich beeilen muss. Seine Schwester Mia schläft noch. Sie hat sich erkältet und bleibt heute zu Hause." Why is Mia at home today?
questions.explanation: "Sie hat sich erkältet" means she has caught a cold. It is Lukas who has to hurry (sich beeilen). Nothing in the text says Mia is bored or did sport.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: "Wie fühlst du dich heute?" Which answer is correct?
choices: Danke, viel besser. Ich fühle mich wieder wohl.
questions.explanation: sich fühlen and sich wohlfühlen need the reflexive pronoun mich after ich. "Ich fühle dich" means "I feel you" (touching), and "Ich bin mich" mixes up sein and a reflexive verb.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Du musst sich beeilen."
questions.explanation: The reflexive pronoun must match the subject. For du it is dich: "Du musst dich beeilen." With a modal verb, the infinitive beeilen at the end is correct, and du musst is the right form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Kannst du ___ bitte konzentrieren?"
questions.explanation: sich konzentrieren with du takes dich. There is no other accusative object, so the dative dir is wrong. mich would mean the speaker, not the person who should concentrate.

questions.stem: Which is the most natural German for "I wash my hands"?
questions.explanation: With a body part as the object, German uses a dative reflexive pronoun and the article: mir die Hände. "mich" is accusative and only works without another object, and sich is the wrong person.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich warte ___ den Bus."
questions.explanation: warten takes auf + accusative: auf den Bus. English "wait for" tempts learners to use für, but "Ich warte für den Bus" is wrong in German.

questions.stem: Complete: "Sie interessiert sich ___ Kunst."
questions.explanation: sich interessieren takes für + accusative. English says "interested in", but German uses für; "in" is a direct translation and wrong here.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich denke oft ___ meine Großeltern."
questions.explanation: denken takes an + accusative: an meine Großeltern. English "think of" suggests von, but "denken von" is used only for opinions (Was denkst du von ihm?) and is less common.

questions.stem: Complete: "Nächsten Monat haben wir Ferien. Ich freue mich schon ___ die Ferien!"
questions.explanation: The holidays are still in the future, so it is sich freuen auf (to look forward to). sich freuen über is for something you already have or that has happened: Ich freue mich über das Geschenk.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich nehme an ___ Kurs teil." (der Kurs)
questions.explanation: teilnehmen an takes the dative, and the dative of der Kurs is dem Kurs (often shortened to am Kurs). "den" is accusative, which is right after denken an but not after teilnehmen an.

questions.stem: Ask a question about "von einem Haus am Meer" in "Ich träume von einem Haus am Meer."
questions.explanation: It is a thing, so use wo + the verb's preposition: träumen von → wovon. woran and worauf use the wrong preposition, and träumen is not reflexive.

questions.stem: Ask about the person: "Ich spreche mit meiner Schwester."
questions.explanation: For a person, keep the preposition and add wem or wen. mit takes the dative, so it is mit wem. Womit is only for things, and wen is accusative.

questions.stem: "Freust du dich auf das Konzert?" Which answer is correct?
choices: Ja, ich freue mich auf es.
questions.explanation: To refer back to a thing after a preposition, use da(r) + the same preposition: auf → darauf. "auf es" is not used for things, and daran and dafür have the wrong preposition.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo Tim, es tut mir so leid! Ich habe mich gestern mit Jana verabredet und total vergessen, dass wir ins Kino gehen wollten. Ich möchte mich bei dir entschuldigen. Kann ich dich am Freitag zum Essen einladen? Ben" Why is Ben writing?
choices: To apologise for forgetting a plan
To invite Jana to the cinema
To say that he is ill
To ask Tim to meet Jana
questions.explanation: Ben forgot the cinema with Tim because he arranged to meet Jana (sich mit Jana verabreden), and he writes "Ich möchte mich bei dir entschuldigen": he wants to apologise to Tim. The invitation on Friday is for Tim, not Jana.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das Kind hat Angst ___ Hund." (der Hund)
questions.explanation: Angst haben takes vor + dative: vor dem Hund. English "afraid of" tempts von, and "vor den" uses the accusative, which is wrong here.

questions.stem: What does "Ich freue mich über das Geschenk." mean?
choices: I'm looking forward to the present.
questions.explanation: sich freuen über means to be pleased about something you have. Looking forward to is sich freuen auf, annoyed about is sich ärgern über, and thinking about is denken an.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Ich interessiere für Fußball."
choices: The reflexive pronoun mich is missing
questions.explanation: sich interessieren is reflexive: "Ich interessiere mich für Fußball." The preposition für is correct, sports usually have no article here, and interessiere is the right ich form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Kannst du ___ helfen?" (ich)
questions.explanation: helfen takes a dative object, and the dative of ich is mir. "mich" is the accusative, the mistake English speakers make because "help me" looks like a direct object.

questions.stem: Complete: "Die Schuhe ___ mir sehr."
questions.explanation: With gefallen, the thing liked is the subject. Die Schuhe is plural, so the verb is gefallen. "gefällt" is the singular form (Der Schuh gefällt mir).

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I miss you"?
questions.explanation: With fehlen the person who is missed is the subject and the person who misses them is dative: "Du fehlst mir" (you are missing to me). "Ich fehle dir" means the opposite: you miss me.

questions.stem: "Wem gehört der Regenschirm?" Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation: gehören takes the dative: the thing is the subject (er = der Regenschirm) and the owner is dative, mir. "Ich gehöre ihn" turns the roles round and uses the accusative.

questions.stem: Complete with the correct order: "Ich schenke ___." (my father, a book)
questions.explanation: With two nouns, the dative (the person) comes before the accusative (the thing): meinem Vater ein Buch. "meinen Vater" is accusative, and the book is the direct object, so it is ein Buch, not einem Buch.

questions.stem: "Hast du Lisa das Buch gegeben?" – "Ja, ich habe ___ gestern gegeben."
questions.explanation: With two pronouns, the accusative comes first: es (the book), then the dative ihr (to Lisa). "ihr es" is English order, and sie is the accusative of Lisa, which is wrong after geben.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir gratulieren dir ___ Geburtstag!"
questions.explanation: gratulieren uses zu + dative for the occasion: zum Geburtstag (zu dem). "für den Geburtstag" is a translation of English "for" and wrong here.

questions.stem: Complete: "Was ___ du mir?" (empfehlen)
questions.explanation: empfehlen changes e to ie in the du and er forms: du empfiehlst, er empfiehlt. "empfehlst" forgets the stem change, and the ich form has no change: ich empfehle.

questions.stem: Read: "Liebe Oma, vielen Dank für das Päckchen! Die Schokolade schmeckt mir sehr gut, und der Schal gefällt Mama total. Nur die Mütze passt mir leider nicht, sie ist zu klein. Kann ich sie meinem Bruder Paul schenken? Er ist erst fünf. Deine Lea" What is the problem?
choices: The hat is too small for Lea.
questions.explanation: "Die Mütze passt mir nicht, sie ist zu klein" means the hat doesn't fit Lea because it is too small. The chocolate tastes good to her (schmeckt mir), and Mum really likes the scarf (gefällt Mama total).

questions.stem: What does "Das Kleid steht dir gut." mean?
choices: The dress is standing up well.
The dress fits in your cupboard.
questions.explanation: stehen + dative, used about clothes, means to suit someone. Belonging is gehören (Das Kleid gehört dir), and fitting in size is passen.

questions.stem: Which is correct for "Give it to me!"?
questions.explanation: Two pronouns: accusative first (es), then dative (mir). "Gib mir es" follows English order, and mich is accusative, which is wrong for the person who receives.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Ich danke dich für die Blumen."
questions.explanation: danken takes the dative, so the person is dir: "Ich danke dir für die Blumen." The reason after danken is für + accusative, so für is correct.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder ___ nächste Woche dreißig."
questions.explanation: werden + an age means to turn that age, and the er form is wird, with no extra -t. "wirst" is the du form, and werdet is the ihr form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Warum ___ du so rot?"
questions.explanation: The du form of werden is irregular: du wirst, with no d. "wirdst" adds the d from er wird, and werdet is the ihr form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Sie ___ Lehrerin geworden."
questions.explanation: werden describes a change, so its perfect uses sein: sie ist geworden. "hat geworden" is the most common mistake; "wird" and "wurde" can't be combined with the participle geworden.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I want to become a doctor"?
questions.explanation: "want" is wollen (ich will), and werden goes to the end as an infinitive. Jobs after werden have no article: Arzt werden. "Ich werde …" means "I become / will become", not "I want".

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich gehe ___ Tag joggen."
questions.explanation: Time expressions with jeder are in the accusative, and der Tag is masculine: jeden Tag. jeder is the nominative, and alle needs a plural noun (alle Tage is unusual here).

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Kinder haben ein Geschenk bekommen."
questions.explanation: Kinder is plural, and jeder only works with singular nouns, so the plural word is alle. With the singular you would say "Jedes Kind hat ein Geschenk bekommen."

questions.stem: Complete: "Hallo Sara! Gibt es etwas ___?"
questions.explanation: After etwas, an adjective becomes a noun: capital letter and the ending -es, so etwas Neues (anything new). Small "neues" forgets the capital, and "neu" has no ending.

questions.stem: What does "sympathisch" mean?
questions.explanation: sympathisch is a false friend: it means likeable, someone you take to. Sympathetic (understanding) is "verständnisvoll"; good-looking is hübsch or gut aussehend.

questions.stem: Read: "Herr Wagner wohnt seit Mai neben uns. Er ist groß, hat graue Haare und trägt eine Brille. Er ist sehr höflich, aber ein bisschen ernst. Jeden Morgen um sechs geht er mit seinem Hund spazieren." Which is true?
questions.explanation: "trägt eine Brille" means he wears glasses. He is ernst (serious), not someone who laughs a lot; the text doesn't mention a beard; and he is groß (tall) with grey hair.

questions.stem: Which answer fits the question "Wie sieht deine Schwester aus?"
choices: Sie ist sehr fleißig und ehrlich.
Sie ist schlank und hat lange Haare.
questions.explanation: "Wie sieht … aus?" asks about appearance, so the answer describes her body and hair. fleißig and ehrlich are character (Wie ist sie?), fernsehen is watching TV, and "Es geht ihr gut" answers "Wie geht es ihr?".

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Park war ganz leer. Ich habe ___ gesehen."
questions.explanation: The park was empty, so you saw nobody: niemand (or niemanden). jemand and alle would mean you saw people, and etwas means something.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Mein Opa hat sehr alt geworden."
questions.explanation: werden forms the perfect with sein: "Mein Opa ist sehr alt geworden." Mein already acts as the article, and sehr alt is correct.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich suche einen ___ Mantel." (warm)
questions.explanation: Mantel is masculine and the object of suchen, so it is accusative. "einen" already shows masculine accusative, so the adjective just takes -en: einen warmen Mantel. "warmer" is the masculine nominative ending (ein warmer Mantel).

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist ein ___ Kleid." (rot)
questions.explanation: Kleid is neuter (das Kleid). "ein" doesn't show that it's neuter, so the adjective takes the -es of "das": ein rotes Kleid. "roter" would be masculine, and "rote" is the ending after "das" (das rote Kleid), not after "ein".

questions.stem: Complete: "Sie trägt eine ___ Bluse." (gestreift)
questions.explanation: Bluse is feminine, and after "eine" in the nominative or accusative the adjective ends in -e: eine gestreifte Bluse. "gestreiften" would be right in the dative (mit einer gestreiften Bluse).

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein ___ Pullover ist kaputt." (alt)
questions.explanation: Pullover is masculine and the subject, so nominative. "mein" looks like "ein" and doesn't show the gender, so the adjective takes the -er of "der": mein alter Pullover. "alten" would be the accusative (meinen alten Pullover).

questions.stem: Complete: "Er geht mit seiner ___ Freundin ins Kino." (neu)
questions.explanation: "mit" takes the dative, and after any dative ein-word (seiner, einem, meinen …) the adjective always ends in -en: mit seiner neuen Freundin. "neue" would be the nominative or accusative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das sind keine ___ Schuhe." (bequem)
questions.explanation: In the plural after keine, meine, unsere and the other ein-words, the adjective ends in -en: keine bequemen Schuhe. "bequeme" is the ending with no article at all (bequeme Schuhe).

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: After sein, an adjective has no ending: Der Rock ist kurz. Before a noun it always needs one: der kurze Rock, ein kurzer Rock. "Der Rock ist kurzer" adds an ending where none belongs (and kürzer would mean "shorter").

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -el drop the e before an ending: dunkel becomes dunkle, dunklen, dunkles. So it must be "eine dunkle Hose". The other three sentences drop the e correctly.

questions.stem: What does "Die Hose ist zu eng." mean?
questions.explanation: eng means tight (or narrow). Too loose would be "zu weit", too long "zu lang", and too expensive "zu teuer". Note that die Hose is singular in German: one pair of trousers.

questions.stem: Read the message: "Hallo Mia! Ich gehe am Samstag zu Tims Party. Ich trage mein neues blaues Kleid und meine schwarzen Stiefel. Leihst du mir deinen warmen Schal? Es ist so kalt! Lena" What does Lena want from Mia?
questions.explanation: "Leihst du mir deinen warmen Schal?" means "Will you lend me your warm scarf?" The blue dress and the black boots are Lena's own (mein, meine), and a woolly hat (eine Mütze) isn't mentioned.

questions.stem: The sales assistant asks: "Möchten Sie die Jacke anprobieren?" Which answer is correct?
choices: Ja, gern. Ich probiere sie an.
questions.explanation: anprobieren is separable: the prefix an goes to the end of the sentence, after the object: Ich probiere sie an. "Ich anprobiere sie" forgets to separate the prefix, and "an sie" treats it like a preposition.

questions.stem: Complete: "Du ___ heute einen schönen Hut." (tragen)
questions.explanation: tragen changes a to ä in the du and er/sie/es forms, like fahren: du trägst, er trägt. "tragst" forgets the umlaut, and "trägt" is the er/sie/es form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der ___ Pullover ist reduziert." (blau)
questions.explanation: After der, die, das in the nominative singular, the adjective ends in -e: der blaue Pullover. "der" already shows masculine nominative, so the adjective doesn't need -er. "blauer" is correct only after ein (ein blauer Pullover).

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich nehme das ___ Hemd." (weiß)
questions.explanation: Hemd is neuter, and neuter accusative after "das" takes -e: das weiße Hemd. "weißes" is the ending after "ein" (ein weißes Hemd), where the article doesn't show the gender.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir fahren mit dem ___ Aufzug." (neu)
questions.explanation: "mit" takes the dative, and after dem, der and den in the dative the adjective always ends in -en: mit dem neuen Aufzug. "neuem" copies the -em of dem, but the article already shows the case, so the adjective doesn't repeat it.

questions.stem: Complete: "Alle ___ Jacken sind im zweiten Stock." (reduziert)
questions.explanation: alle is a der-word, and after der-words every plural adjective ends in -en: alle reduzierten Jacken. "reduzierte" would be correct with no article (reduzierte Jacken).

questions.stem: Complete: "Kann ich diesen ___ Rock umtauschen?" (kurz)
questions.explanation: Rock is masculine and the object, so accusative: diesen. Masculine accusative always has -en on the adjective: diesen kurzen Rock. "kurze" is the nominative (dieser kurze Rock).

questions.stem: Complete the answer: "Welche Hose nehmen Sie?" – "Die ___." (schwarz)
questions.explanation: When the noun is left out, the adjective keeps its ending: die schwarze (Hose), feminine accusative after die, so -e. "Die schwarz" drops the ending, which German never does before an understood noun.

questions.stem: How do you say "a bag made of leather"?
questions.explanation: German uses aus + the material, with no article: aus Leder, aus Holz, aus Baumwolle. "von Leder" is a literal translation of English "of" and sounds wrong.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: umtauschen is separable: the prefix um goes to the very end: Ich tausche die Schuhe um. In the perfect the ge- goes between prefix and verb: Ich habe die Schuhe umgetauscht, so "umtauscht" is wrong.

questions.stem: Read the sign in a department store: "Erdgeschoss: Kasse, Kundenservice. 1. Stock: Damenmode. 2. Stock: Herrenmode, Schuhe. 3. Stock: Spielzeug. Rolltreppe und Aufzug in der Mitte." Where do you find men's clothes?
questions.explanation: Herrenmode (men's fashion) is in the 2. Stock, the second floor. Damenmode (women's fashion) is on the first floor, and the Erdgeschoss (ground floor) has the tills and customer service.

questions.stem: At the till you hear: "Brauchen Sie eine Tüte?" What does it mean?
choices: Do you need a changing room?
questions.explanation: die Tüte is a paper or plastic bag from a shop. A receipt is die Quittung or der Kassenzettel, a discount der Rabatt, and a changing room die Umkleidekabine.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Das schwarzes Kleid ist zu eng.
questions.explanation: After "das" the adjective ends in -e, not -es: das schwarze Kleid. The -es ending belongs after "ein" (ein schwarzes Kleid), where the article doesn't show that the noun is neuter.

questions.stem: You want to exchange a jumper. The assistant asks: "Haben Sie den Kassenzettel?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: der Kassenzettel is the till receipt, and die Quittung also means receipt, so "Ja, hier ist die Quittung" answers the question. die Marke is the brand, der Rabatt a discount, and die Garantie a guarantee.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich trinke gern ___ Wasser." (kalt)
questions.explanation: There's no article, so the adjective takes the ending of the article: Wasser is neuter (das Wasser), so kaltes Wasser. "kalten" is a common mistake: neuter accusative stays -es, just like das.

questions.stem: Complete: "Sie trinkt Kaffee mit ___ Milch." (warm)
questions.explanation: "mit" takes the dative. Milch is feminine, and the feminine dative article is "der", so with no article the adjective ends in -er: mit warmer Milch. "warmem" would be masculine or neuter dative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir brauchen ___ Eier." (frisch)
questions.explanation: Plural with no article in the accusative takes -e, like the article "die": frische Eier. "frischen" is the ending after die (die frischen Eier) or in the dative (mit frischen Eiern).

questions.stem: Complete: "Brot mit ___ Käse ist lecker." (frisch)
questions.explanation: Käse is masculine (der Käse) and "mit" takes the dative. The masculine dative article is "dem", so with no article the adjective ends in -em: mit frischem Käse.

questions.stem: Complete the sign at the market: "___ Fisch aus der Nordsee!" (frisch)
questions.explanation: Fisch is masculine (der Fisch) and the phrase is nominative. With no article, the adjective takes the -er of "der": Frischer Fisch.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich koche gern mit ein paar ___ Freunden." (gut)
questions.explanation: "ein paar" never changes and doesn't count as an article, so the adjective takes the no-article ending. Here it's dative plural after "mit", so -en: mit ein paar guten Freunden.

questions.stem: Complete: "Er ___ das Fleisch in der Pfanne." (braten)
questions.explanation: braten has a vowel change a to ä in the du and er forms, and the er form has no extra ending: du brätst, er brät. "bratet" is a common mistake that forgets the stem change.

questions.stem: What is the perfect of "Ich schneide die Tomaten"?
questions.explanation: schneiden is irregular: hat geschnitten. It uses haben because it has an object. "geschneidet" treats it as a regular verb.

questions.stem: There is a lot of chilli in your soup. Which sentence describes it?
questions.explanation: scharf means spicy (and also sharp). sauer is sour, like a lemon; süß is sweet; frisch is fresh. Don't use heiß for spicy: it only means a high temperature.

questions.stem: You have finished eating in a restaurant and want to pay. What do you say?
questions.explanation: die Rechnung is the bill. die Speisekarte is the menu, die Vorspeise the starter, and das Trinkgeld the tip, which you give, rather than ask for.

questions.stem: Read the menu: "Vorspeise: Tomatensuppe. Hauptspeisen: gebratener Fisch mit frischem Gemüse; Schnitzel mit Pommes; Nudeln mit scharfer Soße. Nachtisch: Apfelkuchen mit warmer Vanillesoße." Anna eats no meat and no fish, and she loves spicy food. Which main course is best for her?
questions.explanation: "Nudeln mit scharfer Soße" is pasta with a spicy sauce, with no meat or fish. The schnitzel is meat, the fish is fish, and the tomato soup is a starter, not a main course.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: alle is a der-word, so the adjective after it ends in -en: alle frischen Tomaten. Without alle it would be "frische Tomaten". The other three are correct no-article endings.

questions.stem: Complete: "Die Stadt ist lauter ___ das Dorf."
questions.explanation: After a comparative (lauter = louder), "than" is als: lauter als. wie is for things that are the same: so laut wie (as loud as). "größer wie" is heard in casual speech but isn't standard.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder ist so groß ___ ich."
questions.explanation: so + adjective + wie means "as … as": so groß wie (as tall as). als goes with a comparative: größer als.

questions.stem: What is the comparative of "alt"?
questions.explanation: Many short adjectives add an umlaut: alt, älter, am ältesten. "alter" forgets the umlaut, and German never uses "mehr" to make a comparative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Dieses Café ist gut, aber das Café am Markt ist ___."
questions.explanation: gut is irregular: gut, besser, am besten. You're comparing two cafés, so you need the comparative besser. "am besten" is the superlative (the best of all).

questions.stem: Complete: "Die Zugspitze ist der ___ Berg in Deutschland." (hoch, superlative)
questions.explanation: The superlative of hoch is höchst-. Before a noun it takes the normal ending after der: masculine nominative, so -e: der höchste Berg. "hohe" is not a superlative, and "höchster" is the ending after ein, not der.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir suchen eine ___ Wohnung." (groß, comparative)
questions.explanation: A comparative before a noun still takes an adjective ending. Wohnung is feminine accusative after eine, so -e: größer + e = eine größere Wohnung. "eine größer Wohnung" leaves out the ending.

questions.stem: Complete: "Im Sommer ist es hier am ___." (schön)
questions.explanation: After a verb, the superlative is am + adjective + -sten: am schönsten. "schönste" is the form before a noun (die schönste Jahreszeit).

questions.stem: Which superlative is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: After -t (and -d, -s, -ß, -z, -sch) the superlative adds an extra e so that you can say it: am ältesten. alt also takes an umlaut, so "am altesten" is wrong, and "am älteren" mixes in the comparative.

questions.stem: What does "Immer mehr Leute wohnen auf dem Land." mean?
choices: More and more people live in the country.
People always live in the city.
Most people live in the country.
People always lived in the country.
questions.explanation: immer + comparative means that something keeps growing: immer mehr = more and more. Most people would be "die meisten Leute".

questions.stem: Read: "Lukas wohnt in Hamburg, Sara in einem Dorf an der Küste. Saras Dorf hat nur 600 Einwohner. Sara findet das Leben auf dem Land ruhiger, aber Lukas sagt, die Großstadt ist interessanter." Which statement is true?
choices: Sara thinks country life is quieter.
Sara lives in a big city.
Lukas finds the village more interesting.
questions.explanation: "Sara findet das Leben auf dem Land ruhiger" means Sara finds life in the country quieter. Sara lives in a village on the coast; Lukas lives in Hamburg and finds the big city more interesting.

questions.stem: Complete: "Welcher Supermarkt ist am ___?" (nah)
questions.explanation: nah is irregular: nah, näher, am nächsten. The superlative has a ch: am nächsten, which also gives the adjective nächste (next, nearest).

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Berlin hat mehr Einwohner als Hamburg.
Mein Bruder ist älter als ich.
Das Dorf ist nicht so laut wie die Stadt.
Der Wald ist mehr schön als der Park.
questions.explanation: German always forms the comparative with -er, even for longer adjectives: schöner, not "mehr schön". mehr is only the comparative of viel: mehr Einwohner.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich lege das Handy auf ___ Tisch."
questions.explanation: Putting something somewhere is movement to a new place (Wohin?), so "auf" takes the accusative. "Tisch" is masculine: auf den Tisch. "Dem" would be the dative, which is for a position (Das Handy liegt auf dem Tisch).

questions.stem: Complete: "Das Handy liegt auf ___ Tisch."
questions.explanation: "liegen" describes where something is (Wo?), so "auf" takes the dative: auf dem Tisch. "Den" is the accusative, used with "legen" (Ich lege das Handy auf den Tisch).

questions.stem: Complete: "Wohin hast du die Flasche ___? – In den Kühlschrank."
questions.explanation: The question is Wohin? and there is an object (die Flasche), so you need the putting verb "stellen" (a bottle stands upright): hast du … gestellt. "Gestanden" is the perfect of "stehen", which has no object and answers Wo?.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich stehe die Lampe neben das Sofa.
Ich stelle die Lampe neben dem Sofa.
Die Lampe stellt neben dem Sofa.
Ich stelle die Lampe neben das Sofa.
questions.explanation: "stellen" + accusative is the action of putting: Ich stelle die Lampe neben das Sofa. "Stehen" can't take an object, "neben dem Sofa" is the dative for a position, and "Die Lampe stellt" mixes up the two verbs (it should be "Die Lampe steht neben dem Sofa").

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir gehen heute Abend ___ Kino."
questions.explanation: Going to the cinema is movement (Wohin?), so "in" takes the accusative. "Kino" is neuter: in das Kino, contracted to "ins Kino". "Im Kino" (dative) means you are already there; "in den" would be masculine.

questions.stem: Complete: "Gestern habe ich das Bild an die Wand ___."
questions.explanation: Here someone hangs the picture up (with an object and the accusative "an die Wand"), so "hängen" is regular: hat gehängt. "Gehangen" is only for something that was hanging (Das Bild hat an der Wand gehangen). "Gehangt" doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Mantel hat den ganzen Winter im Keller ___."
questions.explanation: The coat was hanging there (Wo? im Keller, no object), so you need the irregular perfect: hat gehangen. "Gehängt" is for hanging something up, and "gestellt" needs an object.

questions.stem: What does "Wir ziehen am Montag ein." mean?
questions.explanation: "einziehen" (separable) means to move in: wir ziehen … ein. Moving out is "ausziehen", and getting dressed is "sich anziehen".

questions.stem: Read the ad: "Helle 2-Zimmer-Wohnung im 3. Stock, mit Balkon. Miete 720 Euro plus 160 Euro Nebenkosten. Kaution: 1.400 Euro. Waschmaschine im Keller." What are the 160 euros for?
choices: extra costs such as heating and water, on top of the rent
questions.explanation: "Nebenkosten" are the additional costs (heating, water, rubbish) paid on top of the rent. The deposit is the "Kaution" (1,400 euros), and the washing machine is simply in the cellar.

questions.stem: "Wo ist denn mein Schlüssel?" Which answer is correct?
choices: Er hat auf den Tisch gelegen.
questions.explanation: A key lying somewhere is a position: liegen + dative, auf dem Tisch. "Auf den Tisch" is the accusative (for movement), and "Er legt" is the putting verb, which needs an object. "Er hat auf den Tisch gelegen" mixes the dative verb with the accusative.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Setz dich bitte auf das Sofa.
Das Kind sitzt auf dem Stuhl.
Die Katze sitzt unter dem Tisch.
questions.explanation: "sitzen" is never reflexive. To sit down is "sich setzen": Ich setze mich neben dich. The other sentences are correct: "Setz dich" + accusative (movement), and "sitzen" + dative (position).

questions.stem: The crate is standing between the cupboard and the door. Complete: "Die Kiste steht ___."
choices: zwischen den Schrank und die Tür
zwischen der Schrank und die Tür
zwischen dem Schrank und die Tür
zwischen dem Schrank und der Tür
questions.explanation: "stehen" is a position (Wo?), so both nouns after "zwischen" are dative: dem Schrank (masculine) and der Tür (feminine). "Den … die" would be accusative, for movement with "stellen". Don't mix the cases.

questions.stem: Who is "der Vermieter"?
questions.explanation: "vermieten" means to rent out, so "der Vermieter" is the landlord. The tenant, who pays the rent, is "der Mieter".

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich war ___ zwei Jahren in Berlin." (two years ago)
questions.explanation: "ago" is "vor" + dative, placed before the time: vor zwei Jahren. "Seit" is for something still going on, "für" for a planned length of time, and "in" points into the future.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir wohnen ___ drei Jahren in Leipzig." (we moved there three years ago and still live there)
questions.explanation: Something that started in the past and is still true takes "seit" + dative with the present tense: Wir wohnen seit drei Jahren in Leipzig. English says "for three years", which tempts learners to use "für".

questions.stem: You started learning German two years ago and you are still learning it. Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich lerne Deutsch für zwei Jahre.
Ich habe Deutsch seit zwei Jahren gelernt.
Ich lerne seit zwei Jahren Deutsch.
Ich lerne Deutsch seit zwei Jahre.
questions.explanation: For something still going on, German uses "seit" + dative and the present tense: Ich lerne seit zwei Jahren Deutsch. "Für zwei Jahre" and the perfect tense copy English; "seit zwei Jahre" is missing the dative plural -n.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Zug fährt ___ zehn Minuten ab." (ten minutes from now)
questions.explanation: "in" + dative points forward from now: in zehn Minuten. "Nach" means after an event (nach dem Essen), and "vor" would mean ten minutes ago.

questions.stem: Complete: "Frühstück gibt es ___ sieben Uhr." (from seven o'clock on)
questions.explanation: "ab" marks a starting point: ab sieben Uhr, ab Montag. "Seit" looks back to a start in the past, and "vor sieben Uhr" would mean before seven.

questions.stem: Read the e-mail: "Guten Tag, ich möchte ein Einzelzimmer reservieren, vom 3. bis zum 6. Mai, mit Frühstück. Ich komme mit dem Zug und bin wahrscheinlich gegen 21 Uhr da. Ist die Rezeption dann noch offen? Viele Grüße, Tom Becker" How many nights does Tom want to stay?
questions.explanation: From the 3rd to the 6th of May is three nights (3rd, 4th and 5th); he leaves on the 6th. He wants a single room ("Einzelzimmer") and asks whether reception is still open at about 9 p.m.

questions.stem: At the hotel reception: "Guten Abend! Haben Sie eine Reservierung?" Which answer fits?
choices: Ja, ich bin für drei Nächte.
questions.explanation: "Auf den Namen …" (in the name of …) is the usual way to answer. "Ich bin für drei Nächte" is not German, "Halbpension gegessen" makes no sense, and reserving tomorrow doesn't answer the question.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich bringe die Koffer ___." (upstairs, as a movement)
questions.explanation: "oben" describes a place (Das Zimmer ist oben). For a direction you need "nach oben": Ich bringe die Koffer nach oben. "Unten" and "draußen" are also places, and they mean downstairs and outside.

questions.stem: What does "Ich bin gerade unterwegs." mean?
choices: I'm out and about (on the way somewhere) right now.
questions.explanation: "unterwegs" means on the way, on the road, out and about. It has nothing to do with "unter" (under) in the sense of underground; downstairs is "unten".

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the future with werden correctly?
questions.explanation: A form of "werden" in position 2 and the infinitive at the end: Ich werde dich morgen anrufen. "Morgen ich werde" breaks verb-second order, "anrufen" must go to the end, and the ich form is "werde", not "wird".

questions.stem: Complete: "Komm ___!" (come here, towards the speaker)
questions.explanation: "her" shows movement towards the speaker: Komm her! "Hin" and "hinauf" point away from the speaker, and "weg" means away.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Wir fahren für eine Woche an die Ostsee.
Ab dem ersten Juni arbeite ich hier.
Ich habe das Hotel vor zwei Woche gebucht.
questions.explanation: "vor" takes the dative, and in the dative plural "Woche" becomes "Wochen": vor zwei Wochen. The other sentences are correct.

questions.stem: What is "das Gepäck"?
questions.explanation: "das Gepäck" is luggage (a collective noun with no plural). The passport is "der Pass", the booking "die Buchung" and customs "der Zoll".

questions.stem: Which is the most polite way to ask for help?
questions.explanation: "Könnten Sie …?" (Konjunktiv II) plus "bitte" is the polite request. The imperative and "Sie müssen" are direct, and "Konnten" without the umlaut is the simple past: "Were you able to help me?"

questions.stem: Ordering in a café. Complete: "Ich ___ gern ein Stück Kuchen."
questions.explanation: "Ich hätte gern …" (I would like) is the polite way to ask for something. "Hatte" is the simple past (I had), "wäre" means would be, and "würde" would need an infinitive at the end.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wenn ich reich ___, würde ich eine Weltreise machen."
questions.explanation: An unreal "if" needs the Konjunktiv II of sein: wenn ich reich wäre (if I were rich). "War" is the simple past, "bin" a real condition, and "würde" is used in the other half of the sentence.

questions.stem: Your friend is always tired. What advice do you give?
questions.explanation: Advice uses "sollte": Du solltest mehr schlafen (you should sleep more). "Du würdest mehr schlafen" means "you would sleep more", which isn't advice; the other two aren't correct German.

questions.stem: What does "Konnten Sie mir helfen?" (without an umlaut) mean?
choices: Were you able to help me?
questions.explanation: Without the umlaut, "konnten" is the simple past of "können": were you able to. The polite "could you" is "Könnten Sie", with ö. The umlaut makes the whole difference.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ du mir bitte das Salz geben?"
questions.explanation: With "du" the form is "würdest": Würdest du mir bitte das Salz geben? "Würde" is the ich/er form, "Würden" goes with wir/sie/Sie, and "wurdest" (no umlaut) is the simple past of "werden".

questions.stem: You want to suggest going to the museum. Which sentence fits?
questions.explanation: "Wir könnten …" (we could) makes a suggestion. "Wir mussten" means we had to (past), and the other two are not correct sentences.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, ich würde mitkommen.
Wenn ich hätte Zeit, würde ich mitkommen.
Wenn ich Zeit hätte würde mitkommen ich.
Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich mitkommen.
questions.explanation: In the "wenn" clause the verb goes to the end (hätte). The whole clause is position 1, so the next sentence starts with the verb: …, würde ich mitkommen (verb–comma–verb). Starting the second half with "ich" is English word order.

questions.stem: Read the text: "Mein Traum? Ich wäre gern Koch in einem kleinen Restaurant am Meer. Leider habe ich im Moment kein Geld und keine Zeit. Aber irgendwann mache ich das!" What is true?
choices: The writer would like to be a cook by the sea.
The writer works as a cook by the sea.
The writer has enough money for a restaurant.
The writer never wants to cook.
questions.explanation: "Ich wäre gern Koch" is a wish: I would like to be a cook. He doesn't work as one yet, has no money at the moment, and says he will do it "irgendwann" (one day).

questions.stem: "Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe!" What is a good reply?
questions.explanation: "Gern geschehen!" (my pleasure) is the reply to thanks. "Gute Besserung" is "get well soon" and "Viel Glück" is "good luck".

questions.stem: What does "Ich komme eventuell später." mean?
questions.explanation: "eventuell" is a false friend: it means possibly, maybe. "Eventually" in German is "irgendwann" or "schließlich", and "instead" is "stattdessen".

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: An deiner Stelle würde ich sofort anrufen.
Wie wäre es mit einem Picknick?
questions.explanation: With "sein", use "wäre" directly: Ich wäre gern berühmt. "Würde sein" is clumsy, and here the infinitive isn't even at the end. The other sentences are correct.

questions.stem: Asking permission very politely. Complete: "___ ich hier kurz telefonieren?"
questions.explanation: "Dürfte ich …?" (might I …?) is the Konjunktiv II of "dürfen": past "durfte" + umlaut. "Durfte" without the umlaut means "was allowed to", "Dürften" is the wir/sie/Sie form, and "Dürfe" is not used here.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Es regnet. Deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
Es regnet. Deshalb ich bleibe zu Hause.
Es regnet. Deshalb zu Hause ich bleibe.
Es regnet. Deshalb bleibe zu Hause ich.
questions.explanation: "deshalb" takes position 1, so the verb comes straight after it and then the subject: Deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause. "Deshalb ich bleibe" is English word order.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das Wetter ist schlecht. ___ gehen wir wandern." (we go anyway)
questions.explanation: "trotzdem" (anyway, nevertheless) is for something that happens against expectation. "Deshalb" would mean bad weather is the reason for hiking; "sondern" needs a negative before it, and "weil" would send the verb to the end.

questions.stem: Complete: "Zieh eine Jacke an, ___ frierst du."
questions.explanation: "sonst" means otherwise: put a jacket on, otherwise you'll be cold. "Deshalb" gives a result, "außerdem" adds a point, and "trotzdem" means anyway.

questions.stem: Complete: "Morgen wird es nicht sonnig, ___ bewölkt."
questions.explanation: After a negative (nicht sonnig), the correction "but rather" is "sondern". "Aber" means "but, however" and doesn't correct a negative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich fahre mit dem Rad, ___ ich die Umwelt schützen will."
questions.explanation: The verb "will" is at the end of the clause, so you need a subordinating conjunction: weil. "Denn" would need normal order (denn ich will …), and "deshalb" or "trotzdem" would be followed directly by the verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es regnet stark.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es stark regnet.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, deshalb es regnet stark.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn regnet es stark.
questions.explanation: After "weil" the conjugated verb goes to the very end: weil es stark regnet. After "denn" the order is normal (denn es regnet stark), and "deshalb" gives a result, not a reason.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the most natural word order?
choices: Ich fahre nach Berlin morgen mit dem Zug.
Ich fahre mit dem Zug nach Berlin morgen.
Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
Ich fahre nach Berlin mit dem Zug morgen.
questions.explanation: In the middle of a German sentence the order is time – manner – place: morgen (when) mit dem Zug (how) nach Berlin (where). English puts the place first, which is the tempting mistake.

questions.stem: "Die Wohnung ist zu klein. Außerdem ist sie laut." What does "außerdem" do here?
questions.explanation: "außerdem" means besides, in addition: the flat is too small, and on top of that it's noisy. A result would be "deshalb", a contrast "aber" or "trotzdem".

questions.stem: Read the forecast: "Morgen ist es im Norden bewölkt und windig, am Nachmittag gibt es Regen. Im Süden bleibt es trocken und sonnig bei 24 Grad. In der Nacht sind in den Bergen Gewitter möglich." Where will it be dry tomorrow?
questions.explanation: "Im Süden bleibt es trocken und sonnig": the south stays dry and sunny. The north gets rain in the afternoon, and thunderstorms are possible in the mountains at night.

questions.stem: Complete: "Heute sind es 30 ___. Was für eine Hitze!"
questions.explanation: After a number, "Grad" has no plural ending: 30 Grad, minus 5 Grad.

questions.stem: What does "Strom sparen" mean?
questions.explanation: "der Strom" is electricity (it can also mean a big river) and "sparen" is to save. Wasting energy would be the opposite.

questions.stem: "Es ist so kalt hier drinnen!" Which reply fits best?
choices: Ja, es ist sehr trocken hier.
Ja, deshalb ist es so heiß.
Nein, es ist nicht kalt, aber warm.
Ja, ich friere auch. Mach doch das Fenster zu.
questions.explanation: "Ich friere auch" (I'm cold too) answers the complaint, and closing the window is a sensible suggestion. "Nicht kalt, aber warm" should be "nicht kalt, sondern warm", and the other two don't fit.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Außerdem ist das gut für die Umwelt.
Wir trennen den Müll, deshalb wir recyceln viel.
Es ist nicht kalt, sondern warm.
questions.explanation: After "deshalb" the verb must come next: deshalb recyceln wir viel. The other sentences are correct.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe heute keine Zeit, ins Kino ___."
questions.explanation: After "keine Zeit haben" the second verb goes to the end with zu in front: ins Kino zu gehen. "gehen" without zu is only right after a modal verb (Ich kann ins Kino gehen), and zu always comes before the verb, never after it.

questions.stem: Complete: "Vergiss nicht, die Kundin ___!" (anrufen)
questions.explanation: With a separable verb, zu goes between the prefix and the verb, written as one word: anzurufen. "zu anrufen" puts zu in front as with ordinary verbs, and "an zu rufen" splits it into three words.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: müssen is a modal verb, so the second verb goes to the end without zu: Ich muss morgen arbeiten. "zu arbeiten" adds a zu that modals never take; the other two break the verb-second rule or the bracket.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe vor, ___ um die Stelle zu bewerben."
questions.explanation: The reflexive pronoun in the infinitive clause matches the subject of the sentence, ich: mich zu bewerben. "sich" is the dictionary form (sich bewerben), a common slip; "mir" is dative.

questions.stem: Your colleague says: "Ich muss mich heute leider krankmelden." What does she mean?
choices: She has to see a doctor today.
She is calling in sick today.
She is reporting a colleague who is ill.
She has to work although she is ill.
questions.explanation: sich krankmelden means to tell your employer you are ill and won't come in: to call in sick. It doesn't say anything about seeing a doctor, and she is talking about herself (mich), not someone else.

questions.stem: Complete: "Sie bewirbt sich ___ eine Stelle als Verkäuferin."
questions.explanation: You apply for a job with um: sich um eine Stelle bewerben. "für" is the English pattern ("apply for"). bei is used for the company: sich bei einer Bank bewerben.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder ___ sich bei einer großen Firma."
questions.explanation: bewerben changes e to i in the du and er/sie/es forms: er bewirbt sich. "bewerbt" forgets the stem change, and "bewirbst" is the du form.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says "I hope the boss is coming"?
choices: Ich hoffe, der Chef zu kommen.
Ich hoffe, dass kommt der Chef.
Ich hoffe, der Chef kommt zu.
Ich hoffe, dass der Chef kommt.
questions.explanation: The person hoping (ich) and the person coming (der Chef) are different, so you need a dass clause with the verb at the end: dass der Chef kommt. zu + infinitive only works when both actions belong to the same subject.

questions.stem: Read the note on your desk: "Herr Vogel hat um 10 Uhr angerufen. Er ist für die neuen Verträge zuständig und bittet Sie, ihn heute noch zurückzurufen. Morgen ist er nicht im Büro." What should you do?
choices: Send Herr Vogel the new contracts tomorrow.
Visit Herr Vogel in his office tomorrow.
Wait until Herr Vogel calls again.
questions.explanation: "bittet Sie, ihn heute noch zurückzurufen" means he asks you to call him back today. Tomorrow he isn't in the office, so waiting or visiting tomorrow won't work. He is in charge of the contracts (zuständig für), but he doesn't ask you to send them.

questions.stem: You call a company. "Firma Lindner, guten Tag." – "Kann ich bitte Frau Roth sprechen?" – "Tut mir leid, sie ist gerade in einer Besprechung." What do you say next?
choices: Könnten Sie ihr bitte sagen, dass ich angerufen habe?
questions.explanation: As the caller you leave a message: Könnten Sie ihr bitte sagen, dass ich angerufen habe? "Kann ich etwas ausrichten?" (Can I take a message?) and "Ich verbinde Sie" are what the person answering says, and "Vogel am Apparat" is how you answer the phone.

questions.stem: What does "das Gehalt" mean?
questions.explanation: das Gehalt is the salary you earn (plural die Gehälter). A contract is der Vertrag, a meeting die Besprechung and overtime die Überstunden.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Es ist wichtig, zu pünktlich sein.
Es ist wichtig, pünktlich zu sein.
Es ist wichtig, pünktlich zu sind.
questions.explanation: After "es ist wichtig" the verb goes to the end as an infinitive with zu, and zu stands directly before it: pünktlich zu sein. Without zu the sentence is incomplete, "zu pünktlich" means "too punctual", and the verb after zu is always the infinitive (sein), never a conjugated form.

questions.stem: How do you write "Anna's book" in German? "___ Buch liegt auf dem Tisch."
questions.explanation: With a name, German adds -s without an apostrophe and without an article: Annas Buch. "Anna's" copies English spelling, and "Das Annas Buch" adds an article that this form never takes.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist das Auto von ___ Bruder."
questions.explanation: von always takes the dative, and Bruder is masculine: von meinem Bruder. "meinen" is accusative, and "meines" is the genitive form, which comes without von (das Auto meines Bruders).

questions.stem: The name Max ends in an s-sound. How do you write "Max's bike"?
questions.explanation: When a name ends in s, ß, x or z, German writes an apostrophe instead of adding -s: Max' Fahrrad. In speech most people avoid it and say das Fahrrad von Max. "Max's" is the English spelling.

questions.stem: What does "am Ende der Woche" mean?
choices: at the end of the week
questions.explanation: "der Woche" is a genitive (of the week), so am Ende der Woche is "at the end of the week". The weekend is das Wochenende, a different word.

questions.stem: Complete: "Leider ___ er bei der Prüfung durchgefallen."
questions.explanation: durchfallen is a verb of falling, so like fallen it forms the perfect with sein: er ist durchgefallen. "hat" is the most common mistake; "habe" and "sind" don't match er.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe meine Aussprache stark ___."
questions.explanation: verbessern has the unstressed prefix ver-, so it is inseparable and takes no ge- in the perfect: verbessert. "geverbessert" adds ge- by mistake, and "verbesserte" is the simple past, which doesn't go with habe.

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Ich habe die Prüfung bestanden!" What happened?
choices: She signed up for the exam.
questions.explanation: bestehen means to pass an exam. "Ich habe die Prüfung gemacht" would only mean she took it; failing is durchfallen, and signing up is sich anmelden.

questions.stem: Read the ad: "Spanisch für Anfänger. Volkshochschule Bremen. Dienstags, 18.30 bis 20 Uhr, ab 7. Oktober, zehn Abende. Gebühr: 98 Euro. Anmeldung bis 30. September online oder im Büro. Am Ende bekommen alle Teilnehmer ein Zertifikat." Which statement is true?
choices: You have to register by 30 September.
The course takes place on Tuesday mornings.
Only participants who pass a test get a certificate.
questions.explanation: "Anmeldung bis 30. September" means registration is open until 30 September. The course starts on 7 October (ab 7. Oktober), it runs in the evening (18.30 bis 20 Uhr), and all participants get a certificate.

questions.stem: Mia says: "Ich habe Geschichte studiert." What did she study?
questions.explanation: die Geschichte means both story and history; as a subject you study, it is history. Geography is Erdkunde and art is Kunst.

questions.stem: What is a "Gymnasium" in Germany?
questions.explanation: A Gymnasium is the academic secondary school that ends with the Abitur. It is a false friend: a gym is das Fitnessstudio or, at school, die Turnhalle. Vocational school is die Berufsschule.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich möchte ___ für den Englischkurs anmelden."
questions.explanation: sich anmelden is reflexive with an accusative pronoun that matches the subject: ich möchte mich anmelden. "sich" is only for er/sie/es and sie/Sie, and "mir" is dative.

questions.stem: "Weißt du, wann wir den Test schreiben?" – "___ Frag doch Frau Haas."
questions.explanation: Keine Ahnung! means "No idea!", which fits because the speaker then suggests asking the teacher. Kein Problem answers a request, Gute Besserung is said to someone who is ill, and Herzlichen Glückwunsch congratulates.

questions.stem: Complete politely: "Können Sie mir sagen, wo ___?"
questions.explanation: In an indirect question the conjugated verb goes to the end: wo der Geldautomat ist. "wo ist der Geldautomat" keeps the word order of a direct question, the most common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wissen Sie, ___ ich für den Antrag einen Termin brauche?"
questions.explanation: The direct question is a yes/no question (Brauche ich einen Termin?), so the indirect question uses ob, "whether". "wenn" means if/when and is a typical mistake from English "if"; dass doesn't ask anything.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich lasse mein Fahrrad in der Werkstatt ___."
questions.explanation: lassen works like a modal verb: the second verb goes to the end as a plain infinitive without zu: reparieren lassen. "zu reparieren" adds a zu that lassen never takes.

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe mein Auto reparieren lassen" mean?
choices: I let my car get damaged.
I left my car at the garage.
questions.explanation: lassen + infinitive means getting someone else to do the job: I had my car repaired. If you did it yourself, you'd say Ich habe mein Auto repariert. Leaving something somewhere is lassen without a second verb.

questions.stem: Complete: "Meine Schwester ___ sich die Haare schneiden."
questions.explanation: lassen changes a to ä in the du and er/sie/es forms: sie lässt. "lasst" is the ihr form, and "lass" is the du imperative.

questions.stem: You need cash from your account. What do you do at the cash machine?
questions.explanation: Geld abheben means to withdraw money. einzahlen is to pay money in, überweisen is to transfer it to another account, and sparen is to save.

questions.stem: A message on your answering machine: "Hallo Frau Schulz, hier ist die Autowerkstatt Brenner. Ihr Auto ist leider noch nicht fertig, wir warten noch auf ein Teil. Sie können es am Donnerstag ab 14 Uhr abholen." When can Frau Schulz collect her car?
questions.explanation: "am Donnerstag ab 14 Uhr" means on Thursday from 2 p.m., so in the afternoon. The car isn't ready today (noch nicht fertig), and the message doesn't ask her to call back.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich möchte einen neuen Reisepass ___."
questions.explanation: You apply for a document with beantragen. sich bewerben is for jobs and places, anmelden is for registering (yourself or an address), and melden means to report something.

questions.stem: You call the Bürgeramt and hear a short beeping sound again and again. Your friend says: "Es ist besetzt." What does that mean?
questions.explanation: besetzt means engaged or busy: someone else is on the line. A closed office is geschlossen, and a wrong number is eine falsche Nummer.

questions.stem: The bank employee says: "Einen Moment bitte, ich verbinde Sie mit meiner Kollegin." What is happening?
choices: You are being put through to her colleague.
Her colleague will call you back later.
Her colleague is busy at the moment.
You should call her colleague directly.
questions.explanation: verbinden on the phone means to connect or put through: she is transferring your call. Calling back would be zurückrufen, and busy would be besetzt.

questions.stem: You have just moved into a flat in Germany. "Wo muss ich meine neue Adresse anmelden?" – "Beim ___."
questions.explanation: You register your address at the Bürgeramt (citizens' office) within two weeks of moving in. The Finanzamt deals with taxes and the Standesamt with births and marriages.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Können Sie mir sagen, wann das Amt öffnet?
Ich möchte wissen, ob ich hier parken darf.
Könnten Sie mir sagen, wie viel das kostet?
Wissen Sie, wo ist die Post?
questions.explanation: In an indirect question the verb goes to the end: Wissen Sie, wo die Post ist? The other three sentences all put the verb last correctly (öffnet, darf, kostet).

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe ___ drei Tagen Fieber." (The fever started three days ago and I still have it.)
questions.explanation: For something that started in the past and is still going on, German uses seit + dative with the present tense: seit drei Tagen. "vor drei Tagen" means three days ago, and "für" is the English pattern ("for three days").

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I've been ill for a week" (and still am)?
choices: Ich bin seit einer Woche krank.
Ich war für eine Woche krank.
Ich bin vor einer Woche krank gewesen.
questions.explanation: German uses the present tense with seit: Ich bin seit einer Woche krank. The other sentences use a past tense, which says the illness is over, or use haben where krank needs sein.

questions.stem: Complete: "Sie hat seit drei ___ Rückenschmerzen."
questions.explanation: seit takes the dative, and dative plural nouns add -n: seit drei Monaten. "Monate" is the nominative and accusative plural, the form learners often forget to change.

questions.stem: Give your friend advice: "Du ___ zum Arzt gehen."
questions.explanation: Advice uses the Konjunktiv II form sollte, and the du form is solltest. "Du sollst" means someone has told you to (an order, not advice), and "sollte" is the ich and er/sie/es form.

questions.stem: Tell a friend to take the tablet: "___ die Tablette mit viel Wasser!"
questions.explanation: The du imperative is the du form without du and without -st, keeping the e→i change: du nimmst → Nimm! "Nimmst" keeps the ending, and "Nehmen" without Sie isn't a polite command.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a correct instruction from a doctor to a patient?
questions.explanation: The Sie imperative puts the verb first with Sie after it, and a separable prefix goes to the end: Atmen Sie tief ein. "Einatmen Sie" forgets to split the verb, and a doctor uses Sie, not du.

questions.stem: From a package insert: "Nehmen Sie dreimal täglich zwei Tabletten nach dem Essen. Nehmen Sie nicht mehr als sechs Tabletten pro Tag. Schwangere sollten vorher mit dem Arzt sprechen." How many tablets a day is the normal dose?
questions.explanation: dreimal täglich zwei Tabletten is three times a day two tablets, so six a day, which is also the maximum. "two" is one dose, and "three" is how many times a day.

questions.stem: The doctor asks: "Was fehlt Ihnen denn?" What is a good answer?
choices: Ich fehle heute bei der Arbeit.
Nein, mir fehlt nichts, ich bin krank.
Ich habe seit gestern Halsschmerzen und Fieber.
questions.explanation: "Was fehlt Ihnen?" is the doctor's way of asking "What's the matter?", so you describe your symptoms. The other answers take fehlen literally (to be missing or absent), and "mir fehlt nichts" would mean you're fine.

questions.stem: Someone sneezes next to you. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Germans say Gesundheit! (health) after a sneeze, like "Bless you!". Gute Besserung is for someone who is ill, Prost is a toast, and Entschuldigung is what the person who sneezed might say.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe eine Allergie ___ Katzen."
questions.explanation: An allergy in German is "against" something: eine Allergie gegen Katzen. "für" and "von" are guesses from English ("allergy for", "allergic to"); German always uses gegen.

questions.stem: How do you say "I really ought to do more sport"? "Ich ___ eigentlich mehr Sport machen."
questions.explanation: müsste (with umlaut) is the Konjunktiv II of müssen: "really ought to, would have to". "musste" without the umlaut is the simple past (had to), and "muss" is a plain "must".

questions.stem: What is "der Krankenwagen"?
questions.explanation: der Krankenwagen (literally "sick car") is an ambulance. A hospital is das Krankenhaus, the waiting room das Wartezimmer, and a sick note die Krankschreibung.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist der Kollege, ___ unsere Webseite macht."
questions.explanation: Kollege is masculine, and inside the relative clause he is the subject (he makes the website), so the nominative "der" is right. "den" would be correct only if he were the object, as in "den ich kenne".

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Laptop, ___ ich gekauft habe, war nicht teuer."
questions.explanation: Laptop is masculine, and in the relative clause "ich" is the subject: I bought the laptop, so the laptop is the direct object and takes the accusative "den". "der" is the tempting choice if you take the case from "Der Laptop" at the start of the sentence, but case comes from inside the relative clause.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wo sind die Fotos, ___ wir im Urlaub gemacht haben?"
questions.explanation: Fotos is plural, and the plural relative pronoun is "die" in both nominative and accusative. "das" agrees with the singular "das Foto", but here the antecedent is plural.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Die Sendung, die um acht Uhr anfängt, ist sehr gut.
Die Sendung, die fängt um acht Uhr an, ist sehr gut.
Die Sendung, die um acht Uhr fängt an, ist sehr gut.
Die Sendung die um acht Uhr anfängt ist sehr gut.
questions.explanation: A relative clause sends the verb to the end, and a separable verb joins up again there: "die um acht Uhr anfängt". The relative clause also needs a comma on both sides. The second choice keeps main-clause order; the third splits the verb; the fourth has no commas.

questions.stem: Complete: "Kennst du die Frau, ___ das Video hochgeladen hat?"
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun agrees with the antecedent "die Frau" (feminine), and the woman is the subject of the relative clause, so "die". "das" is the tempting mistake of agreeing with "das Video", which is only the object inside the clause.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist der Freund, mit ___ ich das Programm installiert habe."
questions.explanation: "mit" always takes the dative, and Freund is masculine, so the relative pronoun is "dem". The preposition comes first, before the relative pronoun. "den" is accusative; "denen" is the dative plural.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist alles, ___ ich über das Programm weiß."
questions.explanation: After alles, etwas and nichts German uses "was" as the relative pronoun: "alles, was ich weiß". "das" follows a neuter noun, but "alles" is not a noun; "wer" asks about people.

questions.stem: What does "Ich lade die App herunter" mean?
questions.explanation: "herunterladen" (separable: ich lade … herunter) means to download. To upload is "hochladen", to delete "löschen", to save "speichern".

questions.stem: Which word completes the sentence? "Ich habe mein ___ vergessen und kann mich nicht einloggen."
questions.explanation: You need a password to log in: "Ich habe mein Passwort vergessen" means I've forgotten my password. "mein" also fits only a masculine or neuter noun, but a screen, a comment or a radio make no sense here.

questions.stem: Read: "Morgens höre ich im Auto Radio. Eine Zeitung kaufe ich nicht mehr; die Artikel, die mich interessieren, lese ich online. Die Sendungen, die ich mag, kommen sehr spät, deshalb nehme ich sie auf." How does the writer watch the late programmes?
choices: In the car, on the radio.
Later, because the writer records them.
questions.explanation: "deshalb nehme ich sie auf" means "so I record them": "aufnehmen" is to record. The radio in the car is for the mornings, and the writer no longer buys a newspaper.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Ich kenne einen Mann, den in Wien wohnt und Videos macht."
choices: "wohnt" should be at the start of the clause.
There should be no comma before "den".
questions.explanation: The man is the one who lives in Vienna, so inside the relative clause he is the subject and the pronoun is nominative "der". "einen" is correct in the main clause (Ich kenne einen Mann), but its case doesn't carry over into the relative clause.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to join: "Ich habe eine App. Ich benutze die App jeden Tag."
choices: Ich habe eine App, die benutze ich jeden Tag.
Ich habe eine App, die ich jeden Tag benutze.
Ich habe eine App, was ich jeden Tag benutze.
Ich habe eine App, ich jeden Tag benutze.
questions.explanation: "die App" is feminine and the object of "benutze", so the relative pronoun is "die" (feminine accusative = nominative), and the verb goes to the end. The first choice keeps main-clause order, "was" can't follow a noun in correct German, and the last drops the relative pronoun as English does.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich gratuliere ___ zum Geburtstag!"
questions.explanation: gratulieren takes a dative object: "Ich gratuliere dir". "dich" is the accusative, the most common mistake, because English "congratulate you" has a direct object.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir laden ___ herzlich zu unserer Feier ein."
questions.explanation: einladen takes an accusative object (the guest), and "euch" is the accusative of "ihr". "dir" is dative, which is right after gratulieren but not after einladen. "ihnen" (small i) means them, in the dative.

questions.stem: How do you say "on 24 December" aloud?
questions.explanation: Dates use ordinal numbers. From 20 the ordinal ends in -ste, and after "am" it takes the ending -en: "am vierundzwanzigsten". The cardinal "vierundzwanzig" and the ending -e are wrong after am; "im" is for months, not days.

questions.stem: Which ordinal is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: The irregular ordinals are erste, dritte, siebte and achte. "dreite", "einste" and "achtte" don't exist: achte has only one t. (You may also see the longer variant "siebente".)

questions.stem: Complete: "Hast du schon einen Weihnachtsbaum?" – "Ja, wir haben gestern ___ gekauft."
questions.explanation: The pronoun replaces "einen Weihnachtsbaum" (masculine, accusative object), so it is "einen". "ein" is the article without its ending, and "eins" is the neuter pronoun.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ist das dein Glas?" – "Nein, das ist nicht ___."
questions.explanation: Standing alone for "das Glas" (neuter), the possessive needs the neuter ending: "meins". "mein" is the article form used before a noun ("mein Glas"); "meiner" would replace a masculine noun.

questions.stem: It is 30 December. You say goodbye to a colleague until next year. What do you say?
questions.explanation: "Guten Rutsch!" is the wish for the change to the new year, said before 1 January. On 30 December it's too late for Frohe Weihnachten, Ostern is in spring, and Gute Besserung is for someone who is ill.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ ich ein Kind war, haben wir jedes Jahr bei meiner Oma gefeiert."
questions.explanation: One period in the past (when I was a child) takes "als". "wenn" is for repeated events or the present and future; "wann" is a question word; "ob" means whether.

questions.stem: What do people in the Rhineland usually do at Karneval?
choices: They dress up in costumes and watch parades.
They paint eggs for the children.
They let off fireworks at midnight.
questions.explanation: At Karneval (Fasching in Bavaria and Austria) people "verkleiden sich": they dress up in costumes, and there are parades. Advent candles belong to December, painted eggs to Easter, and midnight fireworks to Silvester.

questions.stem: Read: "Am Samstag, dem 31. Dezember, feiern wir Silvester bei uns. Wir fangen um 20 Uhr mit einem Buffet an. Wer möchte, kann gern ein Kostüm tragen. Könnt ihr mir bis zum 20. Bescheid sagen?" What must the guests do?
choices: Let the host know by the 20th.
questions.explanation: "Könnt ihr mir bis zum 20. Bescheid sagen?" asks the guests to let the host know by the 20th. A costume is optional ("Wer möchte, kann …"), and the buffet is provided by the hosts.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Wir wünschen Sie und Ihre Familie frohe Weihnachten."
choices: "Sie und Ihre Familie" should be "Ihnen und Ihrer Familie".
questions.explanation: wünschen takes a dative person and an accusative thing: you wish something TO someone. So the people must be dative: "Ihnen und Ihrer Familie". "frohe Weihnachten" is correct with no article.

questions.stem: In Germany, when are Christmas presents usually opened?
questions.explanation: In Germany the presents are given on Heiligabend, the evening of 24 December. The morning of the 25th is the British and American custom.

questions.stem: You write to your course teacher, Ms Brandt, whom you call "Sie". Which opening and closing fit best?
choices: Lieber Frau Brandt, … Mit freundlichen Grüßen
Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, … Bis bald!
questions.explanation: This is semi-formal: you know her but say Sie, so "Liebe Frau Brandt" with "Viele Grüße" is ideal. "Lieber" is for a man; "Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren" is for an unknown reader and doesn't match "Bis bald".

questions.stem: Complete the formal opening: "Sehr ___ Herr Wagner,"
questions.explanation: For a man the opening is "Sehr geehrter Herr …"; for a woman "Sehr geehrte Frau …". The ending -er shows the masculine, just like "Lieber Tom".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Es tut mir leid, dass ich habe nicht geantwortet.
Es tut mir leid, dass ich nicht habe geantwortet.
Es tut mir leid, dass ich geantwortet nicht habe.
Es tut mir leid, dass ich nicht geantwortet habe.
questions.explanation: After "dass" the conjugated verb goes to the end, after the participle: "dass ich nicht geantwortet habe". The first choice keeps main-clause order, the most common error.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Auto ist kaputt. ___ komme ich heute mit dem Bus."
questions.explanation: The second sentence is the consequence of the first, so "deshalb" (that's why), followed directly by the verb. "Weil" would send the verb to the end, "Denn" needs normal order, and "Trotzdem" means "nevertheless", which doesn't fit.

questions.stem: Complete: "Entschuldigung, ich ___ mich ein bisschen. Ich bin in zehn Minuten da."
questions.explanation: "sich verspäten" means to be late, and it is reflexive: "ich verspäte mich". "verschieben" means to postpone something, not to be late, and "spät" is an adjective.

questions.stem: What does "Können wir den Termin auf Donnerstag verschieben?" ask?
choices: Can we confirm the appointment for Thursday?
Can we move the appointment to Thursday?
questions.explanation: "verschieben" means to postpone or move, and "auf Donnerstag" gives the new day. To cancel is "absagen", to confirm "bestätigen".

questions.stem: Your friend writes: "Sag mir Bescheid, wenn du angekommen bist." What should you do?
choices: Pick him up when he arrives.
Let him know when you have arrived.
questions.explanation: "Bescheid sagen" means to let someone know. "wenn du angekommen bist" means when you have arrived. So he wants a message from you when you get there.

questions.stem: In an e-mail, what is "der Anhang"?
questions.explanation: "der Anhang" is the attachment: "Im Anhang finden Sie …" means "Please find … attached". The subject line is "der Betreff", and a reply or feedback is "die Rückmeldung".

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Liebe Frau Brandt, kannst du mir bitte die Aufgaben schicken? Viele Grüße"
choices: "Viele Grüße" is too informal for a teacher.
"kannst" should start with a capital letter.
questions.explanation: With "Frau Brandt" you use Sie, so the request must be "können Sie". Mixing a Sie-opening with du is a typical register mistake. "Liebe" is right for a woman, "Viele Grüße" is fine in a semi-formal e-mail, and after the opening comma the next word starts small.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo Mia, es tut mir leid, ich verspäte mich um 20 Minuten, weil mein Bus nicht kommt. Kaufst du die Karten? Ich gebe dir das Geld nachher. Bis gleich! Tom" Why is Tom late?
questions.explanation: "weil mein Bus nicht kommt" gives the reason: his bus isn't coming. He asks Mia to buy the tickets and will give her the money afterwards ("nachher").

questions.stem: Which sentence accepts an invitation?
choices: Ich sage gern zu und bringe einen Salat mit.
questions.explanation: "zusagen" is to accept, the opposite of "absagen" (to decline or cancel). The other sentences cancel, ask to postpone, or say you forwarded the invitation.

questions.stem: Complete: "Bitte antworten Sie ___ bald, die Sache ist dringend."
questions.explanation: "möglichst bald" means "as soon as possible". "möglich" alone is the adjective "possible" and doesn't work before "bald"; "inzwischen" means meanwhile.

questions.stem: How many points do you need to pass the Goethe-Zertifikat A2?
choices: 60 overall, with at least 45 written and 15 speaking
questions.explanation: You need 60 of 100 points, and also at least 45 of the 75 written points and 15 of the 25 speaking points. A good written score can't make up for a very weak speaking result.

questions.stem: What do you write in the Schreiben part of the Goethe A2?
choices: A form and a short letter
An informal SMS (20–30 words) and a semi-formal e-mail (30–40 words)
questions.explanation: Schreiben has two tasks: an informal SMS of 20–30 words and a semi-formal e-mail of 30–40 words, each covering three content points. The form belongs to the A1 exam.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the speaking tasks in the Goethe A2?
choices: Asking and answering questions with word cards
Planning an appointment with your partner
questions.explanation: There is no preparation time and no presentation at A2. The three tasks are questions with word cards, talking about your life, and planning something together.

questions.stem: In the planning task your partner suggests: "Wie wäre es mit Samstag um zehn?" You have a dentist's appointment then. What is a good reply?
choices: Da kann ich leider nicht, da bin ich beim Zahnarzt. Geht es auch am Nachmittag?
Ja, gern, um zehn passt es mir gut.
questions.explanation: A good reply refuses politely, gives a reason and makes a new suggestion, so the conversation keeps going. A bare "Nein" ends it, and accepting would contradict your calendar.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich kann heute nicht kommen, weil ich ___."
questions.explanation: After "weil" the conjugated verb goes to the very end, after the infinitive: "weil ich arbeiten muss" (lesson 3). "muss arbeiten" is main-clause order.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe einen ___ Laptop gekauft."
questions.explanation: Laptop is masculine and the accusative object; after "einen" the adjective takes -en: "einen neuen Laptop" (lesson 9). "neuer" is the nominative after "ein", as in "Das ist ein neuer Laptop".

questions.stem: Complete: "Wohin legst du das Buch?" – "Ich lege es auf ___ Tisch."
questions.explanation: "Wohin?" asks about a movement to a place, so the two-way preposition "auf" takes the accusative: "auf den Tisch" (lesson 13). "auf dem Tisch" answers "Wo?" (where something is).

questions.stem: Which sentence is a polite request?
choices: Könnten Sie mir bitte das Formular geben?
questions.explanation: "Könnten Sie …?" is the Konjunktiv II (lesson 15), the most polite way to ask. "Ich will" sounds demanding, and a statement or bare imperative is not polite.

questions.stem: Complete: "Berlin ist ___ als München."
questions.explanation: The comparative of "groß" adds an umlaut and -er: "größer als" (lesson 12). "am größten" is the superlative, and "mehr groß" is an English-style mistake.

questions.stem: An exam instruction says: "Beachten Sie die Uhrzeit." What should you do?
choices: Look at the clock in the room.
questions.explanation: "beachten" means to pay attention to or note, and "die Uhrzeit" is the time on the clock. The instruction tells you that the time in the text matters for the answer.

questions.stem: In a listening text you hear: "Der Kurs beginnt am Montag um neun, äh, nein, um halb zehn." When does the course start?
questions.explanation: The speaker corrects himself: "nein, um halb zehn". The last information counts, and "halb zehn" is 9:30, not 10:30 or 8:30: German "halb" counts towards the next hour.

questions.stem: What does "Ich verwechsle immer die beiden Wörter" mean?
choices: I always mix up the two words.
questions.explanation: "verwechseln" means to mix up or confuse. To forget is "vergessen", to repeat "wiederholen".

glossary.definition: The main past tense of spoken German: a present-tense form of haben or sein in position 2 plus a past participle at the end of the clause (Ich habe in Köln studiert. Wir sind 2010 umgezogen). It translates both "I studied" and "I have studied".

A helper verb that combines with another verb to form a tense. In the perfect the auxiliary is haben or sein; it takes the person ending and stands in position 2 (or last of all in a subordinate clause: weil ich gegessen habe).

The verb form used in the perfect, placed at the end of the clause: gemacht, gesehen, aufgewachsen. Most participles have ge-; verbs with an inseparable prefix and verbs in -ieren do not (verstanden, studiert).

The German pattern that splits the verb into two parts: the conjugated verb in position 2 and the rest (an infinitive, a separable prefix or a participle) at the end, with everything else in between: Ich habe 2018 in Polen geheiratet.
A regular verb whose stem does not change. Its past participle is ge- + stem + -t (gemacht, geheiratet) and its simple past adds -te (machte, heiratete). Most German verbs are weak.

A verb that changes its stem vowel in the past. Its participle ends in -en (geschrieben, gefunden) and its simple past has a new vowel and no ending in the ich and er forms (schrieb, fand). The forms have to be learned with the verb.

A verb that changes its vowel like a strong verb but ends in -t like a weak verb: bringen – brachte – gebracht, denken – dachte – gedacht, kennen – kannte – gekannt, wissen – wusste – gewusst, nennen – nannte – genannt, rennen – rannte – gerannt.

A verb with a stressed prefix (auf-, an-, um-, mit- …) that splits off and goes to the end of a main clause: Ich stehe früh auf. In the participle -ge- goes between prefix and verb (aufgewachsen), and in a subordinate clause the verb joins up again at the end (weil ich früh aufstehe).

One of the unstressed prefixes such as be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver- and zer-, which never separate from their verb. Verbs with these prefixes take no ge- in the past participle: bekommen, empfohlen, entschieden, erlebt, gehört, verlassen, zerstört.

The one-word past tense: ich war, ich hatte, ich konnte, er ging. It means the same as the perfect but is used mainly in writing and stories; in speech Germans use it for sein, haben, werden and the modal verbs. Weak verbs add -te (sagte), strong verbs change their vowel (ging).
A clause that can stand alone as a sentence. In a German statement its conjugated verb is in position 2: Ich bleibe heute zu Hause.

A clause that depends on a main clause and cannot stand alone, introduced by a word such as weil, dass, wenn, als, ob or a question word. Its conjugated verb goes to the end, and a comma separates it from the main clause: …, weil ich krank bin.

A word that starts a subordinate clause and sends the conjugated verb to the end: weil, dass, wenn, als, ob, falls. If the subordinate clause comes first, the main verb follows straight after the comma: Weil es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.

A word that joins two main clauses without changing their word order: und, aber, oder, denn, sondern. It stands in position zero, so the verb stays in position 2: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.

A question inside another sentence: Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist? It starts with a question word or, for a yes/no question, with ob, and the verb goes to the end. Indirect questions are a polite way of asking.

A question without a question word, which you answer with ja or nein. In a direct question the verb comes first (Kommst du morgen?); in an indirect one it starts with ob and the verb goes to the end (Ich weiß nicht, ob er morgen kommt).

A verb whose object is the same person as its subject, used with a reflexive pronoun: sich waschen, sich anziehen, sich freuen. Many German verbs are reflexive where English is not: Ich freue mich (I am pleased), Ich habe mich erkältet (I caught a cold). Reflexive verbs always form the perfect with haben.
